docs.title: ASP.NET Core Interview Notes
docs.text:
A personal study repository, readable on a phone and printable on paper. Built for two very different modes of use: deep study over weeks, and a 60-minute panic revision the morning of an interview.

Reading on your phone

This site works offline once a page has loaded, has full-text search across every note, and follows your phone's dark mode. In your mobile browser choose Share → Add to Home Screen and it opens like an app.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: File When to open it ROADMAP.md The master index. Every topic, numbered and linked. Start of every study session. CHEATSHEET.md The single page you read in the car park. One-liners only. TRAPS.md Every ⚠️ gotcha in the repo, collected. The highest signal-per-minute file here. DIAGRAMS.md Everything worth drawing on a whiteboard. VERSIONS.md What changed in .NET 6 → 10. Interviewers love a "what's new" question. PROGRESS.md Confidence tracker and spaced-repetition schedule. MY-PROJECTS.md Your own work, rehearsed. The most-asked question in every interview. GLOSSARY.md Every acronym, one line each. practice/QUESTION-BANK.md Q&A drill, answers hidden until you look.

docs.title: Why the filenames look like 4.03- and not 4.3-
docs.text:
The minor number is zero-padded to two digits so files sort correctly in every file explorer. Without padding you get 4.1, 4.10, 4.11, 4.2, 4.3… which is unusable once a section passes nine topics.

The roadmap displays 4.3; the file is 4.03-…. The mapping is obvious and the sort order stays correct forever.

Rule: topic numbers never change. If a topic turns out to be wrong or redundant, mark it deprecated in place. Renumbering silently breaks every link in the repo.

docs.title: Printing
docs.text: Yes — and there are two separate workflows depending on what you want.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
Install Markdown Preview Enhanced in VS Code:

code --install-extension shd101wyy.markdown-preview-enhanced

This is the better choice over the more popular "Markdown PDF" extension because it renders Mermaid diagrams (used in DIAGRAMS.md) and supports @import, which is what makes the whole-book export below work.

docs.title: Printing a file
docs.text:
1. Open the .md file
  2. Ctrl+K V — opens the enhanced preview
  3. Right-click in the preview → Chrome (Puppeteer) → PDF
  4. The PDF lands next to the source file

For a quick paper copy without a PDF step: right-click preview → Open in Browser → Ctrl+P. Browser print gives you the best control over margins and scale.

docs.title: Print-specific notes
docs.text:
• Collapsible Q&A does not print. The question bank uses <details> blocks so you can self-test on screen; a closed <details> prints as just the question with no answer. Before printing the question bank, find-and-replace <details> → <details open>. (That's arguably what you want for a paper copy anyway — read-through, not self-test.)
  • Emoji markers print fine in Chrome-based export. They render as monochrome glyphs in some PDF viewers, which is harmless — the shapes stay distinguishable.
  • Keep code blocks under ~90 characters wide. Anything longer gets clipped in A4 portrait rather than wrapped.
  • Use --- between major topics. MPE turns a horizontal rule into a clean section break, and it gives you a natural place to insert a page break if you want one.

docs.title: Writing a new note
docs.text:
Copy TEMPLATE.md. Every note has the same seven sections in the same order, which matters more than it sounds: once the shape is muscle memory you can jump straight to "Traps" on a file you've never opened and know exactly what you're getting.

Then do three things:

  1. Tick the checkbox in ROADMAP.md
  2. Copy any ⚠️ items into TRAPS.md
  3. Add one line to the nav: block in mkdocs.yml — otherwise the note builds but never appears in the site navigation

docs.title: How this gets published
docs.text:
Every push to main rebuilds the site and deploys it automatically — about 60–90 seconds. There is nothing to run by hand.

To preview locally before pushing:

pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve          # then open http://127.0.0.1:8000

MY-PROJECTS.md and PROGRESS.md are deliberately excluded from the published site — they hold personal project details and a self-assessment of weak topics, and the site is public. That exclusion is the exclude_docs: block in mkdocs.yml. Deleting those two lines would publish them.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet — The 60-Minute Blitz
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Traps · Diagrams

One line per concept. No explanations — if a line doesn't trigger recall, that topic is 🔴 and you should open the full note instead of re-reading this.

This file is a recall test, not a lesson. Read it with the right-hand column covered, if you print it.

docs.title: Middleware order (memorize verbatim)
docs.text:
ExceptionHandler → HSTS → HttpsRedirection → StaticFiles → Routing
→ CORS → Authentication → Authorization → custom → Endpoints

Authentication always before Authorization. CORS before both. Exception handler first so it wraps everything.

docs.title: DI lifetimes
docs.text:
Instance per Typical use Transient every injection cheap, stateless helpers Scoped HTTP request DbContext, unit of work, per-request state Singleton application config, caches, HttpClient factories

Never inject shorter-lived into longer-lived. Background services must create their own scope.

docs.title: HTTP verbs
docs.text: Verb Safe Idempotent Body GET ✅ ✅ ✗ HEAD ✅ ✅ ✗ POST ✗ ✗ ✅ PUT ✗ ✅ ✅ PATCH ✗ ✗ ✅ DELETE ✗ ✅ ✗

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
200 OK · 201 Created (+ Location) · 202 Accepted · 204 No Content 301 Moved · 304 Not Modified 400 Bad Request · 401 Unauthenticated · 403 Unauthorized · 404 Not Found 405 Method Not Allowed · 409 Conflict · 415 Unsupported Media Type 422 Unprocessable · 429 Too Many Requests 500 Server Error · 502 Bad Gateway · 503 Unavailable · 504 Gateway Timeout

401 vs 403: 401 = I don't know who you are. 403 = I know, and you still can't.

docs.title: What [ApiController] gives you
docs.text: Automatic 400 on invalid ModelState · inferred binding sources · ProblemDetails errors · attribute routing required · multipart/form-data inference.

docs.title: Filter pipeline order
docs.text:
Authorization → Resource → [model binding] → Action → [action runs] → Result

Exception filters wrap Action and Result. Scope order: global → controller → action on the way in, reversed on the way out.

docs.title: EF Core loading
docs.text: Include/ThenInclude = eager · lazy = proxies, causes N+1 · Entry(x).Collection().Load() = explicit. AsNoTracking() for every read you won't save. AsSplitQuery() when Includes cartesian-explode.

docs.title: JWT
docs.text: Three base64 parts: header.payload.signature. Signed, not encrypted. Validate: signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf. Short-lived access token + refresh token for revocation.

docs.title: Auth vs authz
docs.text: Authentication = who are you (ClaimsPrincipal). Authorization = what may you do (roles → claims → policies → requirements → resource-based, in increasing power).

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Cache-aside is the default: read cache → miss → read DB → populate → return. IMemoryCache = per instance. IDistributedCache/Redis = shared. HybridCache = both + stampede protection.

docs.title: HttpClient
docs.text: Always IHttpClientFactory. Never new HttpClient() per request. Never a raw static either — it won't see DNS changes.

docs.title: SOLID
docs.text: Single responsibility · Open/closed · Liskov substitution · Interface segregation · Dependency inversion.

docs.title: Async rules
docs.text: Async all the way down. No .Result / .Wait(). No async void outside event handlers. Pass CancellationToken through. ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries only.

docs.title: Isolation levels vs read phenomena
docs.text:
Level Dirty read Non-repeatable Phantom Read Uncommitted ✅ ✅ ✅ Read Committed ✗ ✅ ✅ Repeatable Read ✗ ✗ ✅ Serializable ✗ ✗ ✗

(✅ = the phenomenon can still occur.)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: xUnit [Fact] / [Theory] + [InlineData]. Mock the boundary, not the thing under test. WebApplicationFactory<Program> for integration. Testcontainers over InMemory.

docs.title: The four questions you will definitely be asked
docs.text:
1. Walk me through what happens when a request hits your API. → 25.2. Rehearse out loud.
  2. Explain the DI lifetimes and when each is wrong. → 6.3 + 6.4.
  3. This endpoint is slow. How do you find out why? → 19.15.
  4. Tell me about something you built and what you'd do differently. → MY-PROJECTS.md.

docs.title: Last 5 minutes
docs.text: Read TRAPS.md. Then close the laptop. Cramming new material in the final minutes displaces what you already knew — that's the one thing that reliably makes interviews go worse.

docs.title: Diagrams Worth Memorizing
docs.text:
← Roadmap · README

Every 🎯 topic in the roadmap should end up here. These are the drawings that turn a rambling verbal answer into a confident one — when you can draw it, you stop backtracking, and the interviewer can follow you.

Practise on paper. Being able to read a diagram is not the same as being able to produce one under pressure with a marker in your hand.

Diagrams use Mermaid, which renders in the VS Code preview (with Markdown Preview Enhanced), on GitHub, and in the exported PDF.

docs.title: 1. The ASP.NET Core request pipeline · 5.1
docs.text:
The single most useful diagram in this repo. If you can draw this and narrate it, you can answer a large fraction of every ASP.NET Core interview.

flowchart TD
    A[HTTP Request] --> B[Kestrel]
    B --> C[ExceptionHandler]
    C --> D[HSTS / HttpsRedirection]
    D --> E[StaticFiles]
    E --> F[Routing]
    F --> G[CORS]
    G --> H[Authentication]
    H --> I[Authorization]
    I --> J[Custom middleware]
    J --> K[Endpoint: filters → action]
    K --> L[Response travels back up]
    L --> A

The narration: each middleware gets the HttpContext, does work before calling next(), then does work after it returns. So the pipeline is a nested set of try/finally-shaped calls, not a flat list — which is exactly why order matters and why response-modifying middleware has to be registered early.

docs.title: 2. DI service lifetimes · 6.3
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph App["Application (root scope)"]
        S["Singleton — one instance forever"]
        subgraph R1["Request 1 scope"]
            SC1["Scoped — one per request"]
            T1["Transient"] & T2["Transient"]
        end
        subgraph R2["Request 2 scope"]
            SC2["Scoped — a different one"]
            T3["Transient"]
        end
    end

The narration: transient is per-injection, scoped is per-request, singleton is per-app. The captive dependency problem is what happens when you draw an arrow from S into SC1 — the singleton pins a request-scoped object alive forever.

docs.title: 3. OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE · 15.8
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Client app
    participant A as Auth server
    participant R as Resource API

    C->>C: Generate code_verifier + code_challenge
    U->>C: Click "Log in"
    C->>A: /authorize (+ code_challenge)
    A->>U: Login + consent
    U->>A: Credentials
    A->>C: Redirect with authorization code
    C->>A: /token (code + code_verifier)
    A->>A: Verify challenge matches verifier
    A->>C: Access token (+ refresh token)
    C->>R: Request + Bearer token
    R->>R: Validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry
    R->>C: Protected resource

docs.title: 4. Clean Architecture layers · 22.7
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    I["Infrastructure — EF Core, HTTP clients, file system"] --> A
    W["Web / API — controllers, middleware, DI wiring"] --> A
    A["Application — use cases, interfaces, DTOs"] --> D
    D["Domain — entities, value objects, domain events"]

The one rule: dependencies point inward. Domain knows nothing about anything. The interface for a repository lives in Application; the implementation lives in Infrastructure. That inversion is the entire point — everything else is folder naming.

docs.title: Legend
docs.text:
Marker Meaning 🔥 Near-certain. Asked in almost every ASP.NET Core interview. If you know nothing else, know these. ⭐ Common. Shows up regularly. Expect at least a few of these per interview. 💻 Hands-on. You must be able to write this on a whiteboard or in a live-coding round — describing it is not enough. ⚠️ Trap. A classic gotcha. Interviewers use these to separate people who've read a blog from people who've shipped. 🧠 Senior. Only needed if you're targeting senior/lead/architect roles. Safe to skip for junior interviews. 🎯 Diagram. Worth being able to draw. Practise it on paper.

Checkboxes track "notes written and read." Track your recall confidence separately in PROGRESS.md — the two are not the same thing, and confidence is what actually decays.

Topic numbers are permanent. Once a note file exists at a number, that number never changes. Links below are pre-wired — they will be dead until the corresponding note is written.

docs.title: Traps — Things That Are Wrong In A Way That Sounds Right
docs.text:
← Roadmap · README

This is the highest signal-per-minute file in the repo. Every ⚠️ marker in the roadmap lands here, in one line each, with the correction.

Interviewers use these deliberately. A candidate who's read blog posts gives the plausible answer; a candidate who's shipped gives the correct one. That gap is the whole point of the question.

Read this twice the day before. Then once more in the morning.

docs.title: Async and threading
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "async makes code run on another thread" async/await is about not blocking a thread, not about using more of them. A truly async I/O call uses no thread while it waits. 2.11 ".Result is fine if I know the task is done" In any context with a synchronization context it can deadlock, and in ASP.NET Core it blocks a thread-pool thread. Under load this cascades into thread-pool starvation. 2.13 "async void is fine for event handlers" It's tolerable for UI event handlers and wrong everywhere else — exceptions can't be caught by the caller and will crash the process. 2.15 "ConfigureAwait(false) is needed in ASP.NET Core" ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it changes nothing in app code. It still matters in libraries, which may run on other platforms. 2.13

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "Scoped means one instance per class" Scoped means one instance per scope, which in a web app is one per HTTP request. Background services have no ambient scope — you must create one. 6.5 "Injecting a scoped service into a singleton is fine" The singleton captures that instance forever. Your DbContext becomes an app-lifetime object shared across all requests — non-thread-safe and leaking. 6.4 "Transient services are always safe" A transient registered into a singleton lives as long as the singleton. Lifetime is determined by the consumer, not the registration. 6.4 "The container disposes everything I give it" It disposes instances it created. If you pass an already-constructed instance to AddSingleton(instance), you own disposal. 6.10

docs.title: Middleware and pipeline
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "Middleware order doesn't really matter" UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication means User is never populated — the app silently 401s or, worse, silently allows. 5.2 "I can inject a scoped service into middleware's constructor" Conventional middleware is a singleton. Scoped services go in the InvokeAsync parameters, or use IMiddleware factory-based middleware. 5.6 "I can read the request body in middleware and the controller still gets it" The body is a forward-only stream and is consumed. You need EnableBuffering() and to rewind it. 5.9 "Modify the response after await next()" By then the response may already be sent. Headers can't be changed once the response has started — use OnStarting. 5.8

docs.title: EF Core
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "DbContext should be a singleton for performance" It is not thread-safe and its change tracker grows unbounded. Scoped is the correct lifetime; use AddDbContextPool if you want the pooling win. 13.2 ".ToList() then filter — same thing" ToList() executes the query. Everything after it filters in memory after pulling the whole table across the wire. 13.10 "Lazy loading is convenient and harmless" It's the primary cause of N+1 queries, and it fires queries at serialization time, long after the context you expected. 13.9 "FromSqlRaw with string interpolation is fine" That's SQL injection. FromSqlInterpolated (or FromSqlRaw with parameters) parameterizes; FromSqlRaw($"...{x}") does not. 13.11 "AsNoTracking is a micro-optimization" On read-heavy endpoints returning many rows it's often a large win, and it prevents accidental updates. Default to it for reads. 13.7 "The InMemory provider is fine for testing" It doesn't enforce relational constraints, transactions, or SQL translation — tests pass that production fails. Use SQLite in-memory or Testcontainers. 13.20

docs.title: Security
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "JWTs are encrypted" A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted. The payload is base64 — anyone can read it. Never put secrets in a JWT. 15.5 "Store the JWT in localStorage" localStorage is readable by any XSS payload. An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie is safer for browser clients. 15.12 "You can't revoke a JWT, so it's insecure" You can't revoke a stateless token — that's why access tokens are short-lived and revocation happens at the refresh-token layer. 15.7 "APIs don't need CSRF protection" Cookie-authenticated APIs absolutely do. Bearer-token APIs don't, because the browser doesn't attach the token automatically. The distinction is how you authenticate, not whether you're an API. 17.4 "CORS protects my API" CORS is a browser restriction, not a server-side access control. curl ignores it entirely. It is not authorization. 10.10 "EF Core makes SQL injection impossible" Only for LINQ. FromSqlRaw, ExecuteSqlRaw, and dynamic SQL are all still injectable. 17.2 "Auth works locally, so it works in the farm" Data Protection keys are per-machine by default. Two servers means cookies and antiforgery tokens issued by one are rejected by the other. 17.6

docs.title: Web API
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "PUT and PATCH are basically the same" PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial change and is not necessarily idempotent. 10.2 "POST is idempotent if I write it carefully" POST is defined as non-idempotent. Making a POST endpoint safe to retry requires an explicit idempotency key. 10.13 "I need to check ModelState.IsValid in every action" With [ApiController], invalid models are auto-rejected with a 400 before your action runs. The manual check is dead code. 10.4 "Return the entity — a DTO is boilerplate" Entities leak your schema, invite over-posting, and cause lazy-loading serialization cycles. The DTO is the boundary. 10.11 "404 means the route was wrong" It also means "resource not found" — and returning 404 vs 403 for an unauthorized resource is a deliberate choice about information disclosure. 10.3

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "new HttpClient() per call, wrapped in using" Sockets stay in TIME_WAIT after disposal. Under load this exhausts ports. Use IHttpClientFactory. 19.10 "A static HttpClient fixes it" It fixes socket exhaustion but never picks up DNS changes. IHttpClientFactory handles both via handler rotation. 19.10 "IMemoryCache works fine when we scale out" Each instance has its own cache. Users get inconsistent reads depending on which server they hit. 19.3 "Adding a cache made it faster, done" Without stampede protection, a cache miss on a hot key sends every concurrent request to the database at once. 19.4

docs.title: C
docs.text: ⚠️ The plausible answer ✅ What's actually true Topic "throw ex; and throw; are the same" throw ex; resets the stack trace, destroying the original throw site. Use bare throw;. 1.20 "Structs are always faster than classes" Large structs are expensive to copy, and boxing them undoes the benefit entirely. The guidance is small, immutable, and short-lived. 1.2 "Nullable reference types stop null reference exceptions" They're compile-time hints only. Nothing is enforced at runtime, and data crossing a serialization boundary ignores them completely. 1.15 "Value types always live on the stack" Only as locals. As class fields, captured lambda variables, or async locals they live on the heap. 1.1 "Passing a class means pass by reference" It passes a reference, but by value. Reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable. 1.1 "record means immutable" It means value equality plus with. Immutability comes from init, which the positional form happens to generate. 1.2 "name.Trim(); trims the string" Strings are immutable. Every method returns a new string — you must assign the result. 1.3 "StringBuilder is always faster than +" For a fixed handful of joins the compiler emits one String.Concat, which beats a StringBuilder. Use it for loops and unknown counts. 1.3 "protected internal is the restrictive one" Backwards. protected internal = assembly OR derived (wider). private protected = derived AND same assembly (narrower). 1.4 "Changing a const in a library updates consumers" const values are inlined into the consuming assembly. They keep the old value until recompiled. Use static readonly. 1.6 "readonly makes the object immutable" It only stops the field being reassigned. A readonly List<T> can still be added to. 1.6 "new and override do the same thing" override dispatches on the runtime object; new dispatches on the declared variable type. Same object, two answers. 1.7 "You can call a virtual method from a constructor" Base constructors run first, so the derived override runs before the derived fields are initialised. Null reference exceptions that look impossible. 1.7 "A for loop lambda captures the value" It captures the variable, and a for loop has only one. All lambdas see the final value. foreach is safe since C# 5; for is not. 1.13 "An extension method with the same name overrides the real one" The real instance method always wins, silently. No warning that your extension was ignored. 1.14 "a?.B.C protects the whole chain" Only a. If B is null you still get a NullReferenceException. Every link needs its own ?.. 1.16 "?? handles empty strings" It only checks null. "", 0 and false all pass through as real values. 1.16 "var and dynamic are similar" var is compile-time inference with full type safety and zero runtime cost. dynamic disables type checking entirely. Nothing alike. 1.22 "A finalizer is how you clean up" A finalizer makes the object survive an extra GC cycle and runs at an unpredictable time. It's a last-resort safety net. Use IDisposable. 1.21 "A class primary constructor parameter is a property" In a record it is. In a class it's a private, mutable captured field — not exposed, not readonly. 1.26 "Single() and First() differ only in style" Single() throws if there's more than one match — and to know that, it must scan further. Different semantics and different cost. 2.9 "Enumerating an IEnumerable twice is free" For a deferred query it executes twice. Against a database, that's two round trips. 2.6

docs.title: How to answer the question
docs.text:
Don't recite. Pick two features you've actually used and say what problem they solved for you. Something like:

"We moved to .NET 8 mainly for keyed services — we had a factory-with-a-switch for three payment providers that keyed DI let us delete entirely. And TimeProvider meant we could finally test our expiry logic without an IClock abstraction of our own."

That answer demonstrates currency, judgment, and hands-on use in three sentences. A list of twelve feature names demonstrates that you read a blog post.

If you genuinely haven't used a recent version, say so and describe what you'd want from it — calibration reads better than bluffing every time.

docs.title: 1.1 — Value Types vs Reference Types, Stack vs Heap, Boxing
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Next: 1.2 struct vs class vs record

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A value type holds the real data inside the variable. A reference type holds only an address. The data itself sits somewhere else.
  • When you copy a variable, you always copy what is inside it. For a value type that is the data. For a reference type that is the address — so now two variables point to the same object.
  • "Value types live on the stack" is a common answer, but it is not fully correct. Where the data lives depends on where you declared it, not on what type it is.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Think of a variable as a small box that you write something in.

A value type is like writing a phone number on a piece of paper. If you copy that paper, you now have two papers, each with its own phone number. Change one paper, and the other paper is not affected. They are completely separate.

Value types are: int, double, bool, char, decimal, enum, struct, and record struct.

A reference type is like writing a house address on a piece of paper. If you copy that paper, you have two papers — but both papers point to the same house. If someone repaints the house, both papers still point to that same repainted house. The papers are separate, but the house is shared.

Reference types are: class, interface, delegate, record, string, arrays, and object.

This is the most common C# question in interviews. Interviewers ask it because it predicts a very real bug: writing a method that accidentally changes the caller's object.

docs.title: What happens when you copy
docs.text:
// Value type — like copying the phone number
int a = 5;
int b = a;      // b now holds its own copy of the number 5
b = 10;         // we change b
                // a is STILL 5 — the two are unrelated

// Reference type — like copying the house address
var p1 = new Person { Name = "Ada" };
var p2 = p1;    // p2 now holds the same address as p1
                // both point to ONE Person object
p2.Name = "Grace";

// p1.Name is now "Grace" too!
// We never touched p1, but p1 and p2 are the same object.

That second example is the one that causes real bugs. You pass an object into a method, the method changes it, and suddenly your original object has changed too.

docs.title: Stack vs heap
docs.text:
You will often hear: "value types go on the stack, reference types go on the heap."

First, what are these two words?

  • Stack — a small, very fast area of memory. It works like a stack of plates: the last thing you put on is the first thing you take off. When a method finishes, everything it put on the stack disappears automatically.
  • Heap — a bigger area of memory where objects live. Things here stay until the garbage collector decides nobody is using them any more.

Now, the simple answer is mostly true, but an interviewer may push back on it. Here is the fuller picture:

Where you declared it Where it actually lives An int inside a method (a local variable) Stack An int that is a field inside a class Heap — inside that object An int captured by a lambda Heap — inside a hidden closure object An int in an async method, used after an await Heap — inside the state machine object A Person variable inside a method (the address itself) Stack The actual Person object Heap

So a value type follows whatever is holding it. If a class lives on the heap, its int fields live on the heap too — they are part of that object.

The safer thing to say in an interview: value types have copy behaviour and reference types have shared behaviour. That is what C# actually promises. Stack versus heap is a detail of how the runtime happens to do it, and the C# specification deliberately does not guarantee it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Stack["Stack (fast, temporary)"]
        A["a = 5<br/>(the actual number)"]
        B["p1 = address 0x4A2"]
        C["p2 = address 0x4A2"]
    end
    subgraph Heap["Heap (objects live here)"]
        D["0x4A2<br/>Person { Name = 'Ada' }"]
    end
    B --> D
    C --> D

Notice that p1 and p2 are two separate boxes on the stack, but both arrows point to the same single object on the heap.

docs.title: Boxing and unboxing
docs.text:
Sometimes C# needs to treat a value type as if it were an object. To do that, it wraps the value in a small box on the heap. That is called boxing. Taking it back out again is unboxing.

int i = 42;
object boxed = i;         // BOXING: creates a new object on the heap
                          // and copies 42 into it
int back = (int)boxed;    // UNBOXING: checks the type, then copies 42 back out

Why should you care? Because boxing costs memory and time, and nothing in the code tells you it is happening. There is no keyword, no warning. It just quietly allocates.

Here is where it sneaks in:

ArrayList list = new();
list.Add(42);                    // BOXES. ArrayList stores everything as object.

List<int> generic = new();
generic.Add(42);                 // No boxing. The list knows it holds int.

Console.WriteLine("Val: " + 42); // BOXES. The int must become an object
                                 // to be joined with a string.

This is actually the main reason generics were added to C#. Before generics, every collection stored object, so every number you put in a list got boxed. Generics let the collection know the real type, so no boxing is needed. If an interviewer asks "why do we have generics?", this is a strong part of the answer.

docs.title: Equality — what does == compare?
docs.text:
• Value types compare the actual data.
  • Reference types compare the address — meaning "are these literally the same object?"
5 == 5                                   // true — same number

new Person("Ada") == new Person("Ada")   // false!
// Two separate objects. Same contents, but different addresses.

"abc" == "abc"                           // true
// string is special — see below

string is the confusing one. It is a reference type, but it compares by content, not by address. The string type deliberately changes what == does. More on that in 1.3.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
This example shows all four cases you might be asked about. Read the comments carefully — case 3 is the one people get wrong.

// Case 1: pass a value type
static void MutateValue(int x) => x = 99;

// Case 2: change the object a reference points to
static void MutateReference(Person p) => p.Name = "Changed";

// Case 3: point the parameter at a brand new object
static void ReassignReference(Person p) => p = new Person { Name = "New" };

// Case 4: pass the variable itself, not a copy
static void MutateWithRef(ref int x) => x = 99;

Now let us call them:

var n = 1;

MutateValue(n);
// n is STILL 1.
// The method got its own copy of the number. It changed the copy.

MutateWithRef(ref n);
// n is now 99.
// 'ref' means "here is the actual variable, not a copy".

var person = new Person { Name = "Ada" };

MutateReference(person);
// person.Name is now "Changed".
// The method got a copy of the ADDRESS, but the address points
// to the same object. So changing the object is visible outside.

ReassignReference(person);
// person.Name is STILL "Changed" — NOT "New".
// The method changed its own copy of the address to point somewhere new.
// Our 'person' variable still holds the OLD address.

That last case trips up a lot of people. Here is the key idea in one sentence:

With a reference type, you can change the object, but you cannot swap which object the caller is looking at — unless you use ref.

Going back to the paper analogy: you can go to the house and repaint it (everyone sees the change). But if you scribble a different address on your own copy of the paper, that does not change what is written on my paper.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a value type and a reference type?

A value type stores the actual data inside the variable, so when you assign it to another variable, the data gets copied. The two are then completely independent. A reference type stores an address that points to an object on the heap. When you assign it, you copy the address — so both variables now point to the same object, and changing it through one is visible through the other. Value types are things like int, struct and enum. Reference types are classes, interfaces, delegates, arrays and string.

Q: Do value types always live on the stack?

No, and that is a common oversimplification. A value type declared as a local variable inside a method usually does live on the stack. But if it is a field inside a class, it lives on the heap as part of that object. The same is true if a lambda captures it, or if it survives across an await in an async method — in both cases the compiler moves it into a hidden object on the heap. What the language actually guarantees is copy behaviour, not a storage location.

Q: What is boxing and why does it matter?

Boxing is when the runtime wraps a value type in an object on the heap so it can be used where an object is expected. It costs a memory allocation plus a copy, and unboxing costs a type check plus another copy. It matters because it is completely invisible in the code — there is no keyword and no warning — so it is easy to do accidentally in a loop and create a lot of garbage. Using a non-generic collection like ArrayList, or storing a number in an object, will both box. Avoiding this was one of the main reasons generics were added to C#.

Q: If I pass an object into a method and the method assigns a new object to the parameter, does the caller see the change?

No. The reference is passed by value, which means the method gets its own copy of the address. Assigning a new object to that copy only changes the method's local parameter — the caller's variable still holds the original address. But if the method changes a property on the object instead of replacing it, the caller will see that, because both are looking at the same object. To actually replace the caller's object you would need to declare the parameter as ref Person.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "Value types are on the stack." Only when they are local variables. As class fields, captured lambda variables, or async locals, they are on the heap.
  • "Passing a class is pass by reference." It is passing a reference, but the reference itself is passed by value. That difference only shows up when you reassign the parameter — which is exactly when it bites.
  • string looks like a value type. It is a reference type, but it cannot be changed and it compares by content. So it behaves like a value type most of the time, which makes the times it does not behave that way very confusing.
  • Boxing is completely silent. object o = 42; allocates. So does IComparable c = 42;. Nothing warns you.
  • Mutable structs are dangerous. A struct you can change is a known trap, because you can easily end up changing a copy without realising. Covered in 1.2.

docs.title: 1.2 — struct vs class vs record vs record struct
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.1 Value vs reference types · Next: 1.3 Strings

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• There are two separate questions. First: is it copied or shared? (struct = copied, class = shared). Second: how does == compare it? (record = by content, normal class = by address).
  • class is your default. Only use struct when the thing is small, never changes, and does not live long.
  • A record is not a new kind of type. It is just a class where the compiler writes some extra code for you.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
C# gives you four ways to declare a type. It sounds like a lot, but it is really just two yes/no questions combined.

Question 1: When I assign this to another variable, is the data copied or shared? - Copied → struct - Shared → class

Question 2: When I use ==, does it compare the contents or check if they are the same object? - Compares contents → add the word record - Checks if same object → do not add record

Put those together and you get four combinations:

Shared (reference) Copied (value) == checks same object class — == compares contents record record struct (struct, compares contents but slowly) — struct

That last row needs a note. A plain struct does compare by contents, but it does so in a slow way behind the scenes (it uses reflection, which means inspecting the type at runtime). A record struct gets fast comparison code written by the compiler instead.

docs.title: class — the default
docs.text:
This is a reference type. Two variables can point to the same object. == checks whether they are the same object, not whether they look the same.

Use a class unless you have a specific reason not to. The advice is not "use structs for speed" — it is "use classes, and switch only when you can explain why."

docs.title: struct — copied every time
docs.text:
A struct is a value type. Every time you assign it, pass it to a method, or return it, the whole thing gets copied.

It cannot inherit from another struct or class (though it can implement interfaces), and it cannot be null unless you write it as Point?.

Microsoft's rule of thumb for when a struct is a good idea — all four should be true:

  1. It represents one single value (like a point, or an amount of money).
  2. It is small — around 16 bytes or less.
  3. It never changes after it is created.
  4. It will not get boxed often. (Boxing means being wrapped in an object — see 1.1.)

If any one of these is false, use a class.

docs.title: record — a class with free extra code
docs.text:
When you write record, the compiler automatically writes several things for you that you would otherwise type by hand:

  • Equals, GetHashCode, and == that compare the property values
  • a ToString that prints out the properties (very useful when debugging)
  • a Deconstruct method, so you can split it into separate variables
  • support for with, which makes a copy with one property changed
public record Person(string FirstName, string LastName);

var a = new Person("Ada", "Lovelace");
var b = new Person("Ada", "Lovelace");

a == b;
// TRUE. These are two different objects in memory,
// but a record compares the values inside them.
// A normal class would say false here.

var c = a with { LastName = "Byron" };
// Creates a NEW Person. FirstName is copied from 'a' automatically.
// 'a' itself is not changed at all.
Console.WriteLine(a);   // Person { FirstName = Ada, LastName = Lovelace }
Console.WriteLine(c);   // Person { FirstName = Ada, LastName = Byron }

Notice the ToString output. You get that for free — with a normal class you would just see the type name.

When you write a record in that short form (with the properties in brackets after the name), those properties are init-only. That means you can set them when creating the object and never again. So records are immutable by default. See 1.6.

docs.title: record struct — copied and compares by content
docs.text:
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);

This gives you three good things at once:

  • no heap allocation, because it is a struct
  • content-based comparison, because it is a record
  • cannot be changed, because of readonly

That combination is a great fit for small domain values like money, coordinates, or measurements.

The readonly keyword here matters for speed too. When the compiler knows a struct can never change, it does not need to make protective copies of it when passing it around.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Here is how each one looks in real code, and why:

// CLASS — an entity. It has an identity, it changes over time,
// and it has behaviour (methods that do things).
public class Order
{
    public Guid Id { get; init; }
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; } = [];
    public void AddLine(OrderLine line) => Lines.Add(line);
}

// RECORD — a data carrier. It just holds values and gets passed around.
// Perfect for API request/response models, messages, query results.
public record CustomerDto(Guid Id, string Name, string Email);

// READONLY RECORD STRUCT — a small value that never changes.
// No heap allocation, compares by content.
public readonly record struct Point(double X, double Y);

// PLAIN STRUCT — rare. Only when you need exact control over
// memory layout, usually for talking to non-.NET code.
public struct RawHeader
{
    public int Length;
    public int Flags;
}

docs.title: The mutable struct trap
docs.text:
This is worth understanding because it shows why the advice is "make structs readonly".

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Increment() => Value++;
}

Now watch what happens with two almost identical lines:

var list = new List<Counter> { new Counter() };
list[0].Increment();
// This does NOT COMPILE.
// A List's indexer RETURNS A COPY of the struct.
// C# stops you, because incrementing a copy would do nothing useful.

var array = new Counter[1];
array[0].Increment();
// This DOES compile, and it DOES work.
// An array indexer gives you direct access to the element itself,
// not a copy. So the increment sticks.

Same-looking code, two different outcomes. The compiler saved you in one case and not the other. This is exactly the kind of surprise that makes people say "just make structs readonly" — if the struct cannot change at all, this whole problem disappears.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use a struct instead of a class?

When the type is one small value that never changes and does not live very long — something like a point, a money amount, or a date range. The benefit is that you avoid allocating memory on the heap, which means less work for the garbage collector. But it is easy to get wrong. A big struct is slow because it gets copied every single time you pass it around. And if it ends up boxed — wrapped in an object — you have paid for an allocation anyway and gained nothing. So the default should stay class.

Q: What does record actually give you over a class?

The compiler writes four things for you: equality that compares the values inside, a readable ToString, deconstruction, and the with expression for making a modified copy. Underneath it is still a class — same reference behaviour, same heap allocation. What changes is how equality works and the fact that properties are init-only by default. It is the right choice for anything you would describe as "a bag of data": DTOs, API models, messages, events.

Q: Are records immutable?

The short form with properties in brackets is, because the compiler makes those properties init-only. But you can also write a record with normal settable properties, and then it is fully mutable. So record does not mean "immutable" — it means "value equality plus with support". Immutability comes from init, which the short form happens to use.

Q: What is the problem with a mutable struct?

You can end up changing a copy without realising it, because structs get copied whenever they are passed around or returned from a property or an indexer. The clearest example is that calling a method that changes a struct through a List indexer will not even compile, but doing exactly the same thing through an array does compile and does work — because an array gives you the element itself while a list gives you a copy. Making the struct readonly removes the entire category of bug.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "Structs are faster than classes." Only for small, short-lived values. A big struct gets copied on every assignment and every method call, which can easily be slower than one heap allocation.
  • Boxing cancels the benefit. Putting a struct in a non-generic collection, or using it through a non-generic interface, allocates on the heap anyway.
  • record does not mean immutable. It means value equality plus with.
  • A plain struct's built-in Equals is slow. It inspects the type at runtime. Either write your own or use record struct.
  • Record equality includes every field — including collections, compared by address. So two records that both contain a list with the same items will be reported as not equal, because the two lists are different objects. Records are best for simple data.

docs.title: 1.3 — String Immutability, StringBuilder, Interning
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.2 struct vs class vs record · Next: 1.4 Access modifiers

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A string can never be changed once created. Every method that looks like it changes a string actually creates a brand new one.
  • Joining strings inside a loop is slow in a way that gets worse and worse. Use StringBuilder when you do not know how many times you will join.
  • Interning means C# stores just one copy of each identical text written directly in your code, to save memory.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
string is a class, so it is a reference type. But it behaves like a value type in the two ways you notice day to day:

  1. == compares the text, not whether they are the same object.
  2. You cannot change it after it is made.

That second point — immutability — is the root of everything else in this note. Once you really believe "strings never change", the rest follows naturally.

docs.title: Every string operation makes a new string
docs.text:
string s = "hello";

s.ToUpper();
// This does NOT change s.
// It creates a NEW string "HELLO" and returns it.
// We threw that new string away, so nothing happened.

s = s + " world";
// This creates a NEW string "hello world"
// and points s at it. The old "hello" is now garbage.

s.Replace('l', 'L');
// Again — creates a new string, returns it, we ignore it.

Here is the classic beginner bug, and it is worth recognising instantly:

string name = "  Ada  ";

name.Trim();
// Does nothing useful! Trim() returns a trimmed copy,
// but we never stored it. 'name' still has the spaces.

name = name.Trim();
// Correct. We store the new string back into name.

docs.title: Why joining strings in a loop is slow
docs.text:
string result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
    result += i;

Because strings cannot change, each += has to:

  1. work out how long the new string will be
  2. allocate a brand new string of that size
  3. copy everything accumulated so far into it
  4. copy the new bit on the end
  5. throw the old string away

So on loop number 5,000 it is copying 5,000 characters. On loop 9,000 it is copying 9,000. The total work grows like the square of the number of loops. Programmers call this O(n²) — meaning if you double the input, the work goes up four times.

You also create 10,000 dead strings for the garbage collector to clean up.

StringBuilder fixes this. It keeps one internal buffer (a resizable array of characters) and writes into it directly:

var sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
    sb.Append(i);              // writes into the existing buffer

string result = sb.ToString();  // ONE string created, right at the end

But do not use StringBuilder for everything. If you are joining a fixed, small number of pieces, plain + is actually faster:

var greeting = "Hello, " + firstName + " " + lastName + "!";

The compiler is smart here. It turns that whole line into a single String.Concat call, which allocates exactly one string. A StringBuilder would be more code and slightly slower.

The rule: loops and unknown counts → StringBuilder. A fixed handful of pieces → plain + or string interpolation.

Two other options worth knowing:

string.Join(", ", items);         // best when joining a collection
$"Hello {name}, you are {age}";   // interpolation — clear and efficient

docs.title: Interning — sharing identical text
docs.text:
.NET keeps a pool (a shared list) of every piece of text written directly in your source code. If the same text appears twice, both places point at the same single string object in memory. This is called interning, and it saves memory.

string a = "hello";
string b = "hello";
ReferenceEquals(a, b);
// TRUE — both point to the same object.
// The compiler saw the same text twice and reused it.

string c = new string("hello".ToCharArray());
ReferenceEquals(a, c);
// FALSE — this string was built while the program was running,
// so it did not come from the pool.

ReferenceEquals(a, string.Intern(c));
// TRUE — string.Intern() looks the text up in the pool
// and gives you back the shared copy.

string d = "hel" + "lo";
ReferenceEquals(a, d);
// TRUE — both pieces are known at compile time,
// so the compiler joins them before the program even runs.

Be careful with string.Intern. Anything you put in the pool stays there for the entire life of the program and can never be garbage collected. Interning user input is effectively a memory leak that grows forever.

docs.title: Comparing strings properly
docs.text:
a == b                                              // compares the text
a.Equals(b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)     // ignore upper/lower case
string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.Ordinal)       // exact, character by character
ReferenceEquals(a, b)                               // same object? rarely useful

Always say how you want to compare. Some string methods use the current culture — the language and region settings of the machine running the code. That means the same code can give different answers on different computers.

The famous example is Turkish. In Turkish, the capital of "i" is "İ", not "I". So "file".ToUpper() gives "FİLE" on a Turkish machine, and a comparison against "FILE" fails. Real systems have broken this way.

Simple guide: - Comparing IDs, keys, file paths, or anything the computer uses → StringComparison.Ordinal - Sorting or comparing text a human will read → culture-aware comparison

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
// BAD: slow, and creates thousands of dead strings
var csv = "";
foreach (var row in rows)
    csv += row + ",";

// GOOD: one buffer, one string at the end
var sb = new StringBuilder();
foreach (var row in rows)
    sb.Append(row).Append(',');
var csv = sb.ToString();

// BEST for this specific job — clearer and handles the separator for you
var csv = string.Join(",", rows);

// FINE — fixed number of pieces, compiler makes this one Concat call
var greeting = "Hello, " + firstName + " " + lastName + "!";

// SAFE comparison — same result on every machine, in every country
if (string.Equals(input, "admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
{
    // ...
}

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why are strings immutable in .NET?

There are three reasons and they support each other. First, thread safety — if a string can never change, many threads can read it at the same time with no locking at all. Second, it makes interning and hash-code caching possible — a string can safely be a dictionary key, because its hash can never go stale. Third, security — if you validate a file path and pass it to a method, that method cannot change it behind your back after the check has passed.

Q: What is the difference between string and StringBuilder?

A string cannot be changed, so every modification creates a whole new string and copies the old contents across. In a loop, that means the work grows with the square of the number of iterations. StringBuilder keeps one internal buffer and writes into it, growing it when needed, so the work grows in a straight line. But for a small fixed number of joins, plain + is actually better, because the compiler collapses the whole expression into a single String.Concat call that allocates once.

Q: What is string interning?

.NET keeps a pool of the text literals written in your source code, so if the same text appears in several places they all share one object in memory. That saves memory for repeated text. Literals go in automatically. Strings built while the program runs do not, though you can add them with string.Intern. You usually should not, because the pool is never cleaned up — anything you intern lives for the whole life of the process.

Q: Does == on strings compare the text or the object?

The text. string specifically overrides == to compare contents, which is an exception to how reference types normally behave. That exception exists because comparing two strings by memory address is almost never what anyone actually wants. If you genuinely need to know whether they are the same object, you use ReferenceEquals.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• name.Trim(); on its own line does nothing. String methods return a new string. They never change the one you called them on. Always assign the result.
  • StringBuilder for two or three joins is slower, not faster. The compiler already optimises fixed concatenation.
  • Default comparison can depend on the machine's language settings. ToLower(), ToUpper() and some Compare overloads use the current culture. Pass StringComparison.Ordinal for anything the computer uses internally.
  • string.Intern on user input leaks memory. The pool is never cleaned.
  • null, "" and " " are three different things. Use string.IsNullOrEmpty or string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace rather than comparing against "".
  • Length counts storage units, not visible characters. Strings are stored as UTF-16, so an emoji or a character from many scripts counts as 2 or more.

docs.title: 1.4 — Access Modifiers
docs.text:

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• There are six. The two double-word ones catch people out: protected internal means "either one" and private protected means "both together".
  • If you write nothing: class members are private, and top-level classes are internal.
  • internal is the one people forget. It lets you hide things from other projects without hiding them from your own code.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Access modifiers answer one question: who is allowed to see this?

Before the list, two words you need:

  • Assembly — one compiled project. One .dll or .exe file. If your solution has MyApp.Web and MyApp.Core as separate projects, those are two assemblies.
  • Derived type — a class that inherits from your class.

Interviewers mostly ask this to check you know the two double-word modifiers and the defaults, because those are the parts nobody looks up.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Modifier Who can see it public Everyone, everywhere private Only code inside the same class protected The same class, and any class that inherits from it (even in another project) internal Any code in the same project protected internal Same project, OR any inheriting class anywhere private protected Only inheriting classes that are also in the same project

docs.title: The two confusing ones
docs.text:
Read these slowly, because most people guess them backwards.

protected internal = protected OR internal. You get in if you are in the same project, or if you inherit from the class. Either one is enough. This makes it more open than protected alone or internal alone.

private protected = protected AND internal. You need both: you must inherit from the class and be in the same project. This makes it more closed than either one alone.

A memory trick that survives interview nerves:

protected internal opens the door wider. private protected narrows it.

The word private in the second one is your hint that it is the restrictive one.

docs.title: What happens if you write nothing
You cannot leak a hidden type through a visible one
docs.text:
The compiler stops you from exposing something more private than the thing exposing it:

internal class Config { }

public class Service
{
    public Config GetConfig() => new();
    // ERROR!
    // The method is public, so anyone can call it.
    // But it returns Config, which is internal — outsiders
    // cannot even name that type. The compiler blocks this.
}

docs.title: Testing internal classes
docs.text:
internal is not a locked door. You can open it to specific projects, which is the normal way to unit-test internal classes:

<!-- In your .csproj file -->
<ItemGroup>
  <InternalsVisibleTo Include="MyApp.Tests" />
</ItemGroup>

Now the test project can see internal types, but nobody else can. Knowing this is a small but real credibility signal in an interview, because the common bad answer is "I make things public so I can test them" — which permanently widens your API just for testing convenience.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
public class Account
{
    // Nobody outside this class needs to know how we store the balance
    private decimal _balance;

    // Subclasses need this, and they might live in another project
    protected string AccountNumber { get; init; } = "";

    // Other classes in THIS project use it. Outside consumers do not.
    internal Guid InternalId { get; init; }

    // The actual public contract
    public decimal Balance => _balance;

    // Only subclasses, and only ones inside this project
    private protected virtual void Audit() { }

    // Anyone in this project, OR any subclass anywhere
    protected internal virtual void Reset() { }
}

One extra thing worth knowing — a property can have different access on get and set:

public string Name { get; private set; }
// Anyone can READ Name.
// Only code inside this class can CHANGE it.

This is a very common and useful pattern, and people often forget it exists.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between protected internal and private protected?

protected internal means "either one is enough" — you can reach it from anywhere in the same project, or from a class that inherits from it in any project. That makes it more open than either part on its own. private protected means "you need both" — only inheriting classes that are also in the same project can reach it, which makes it more restrictive than either part. private protected was added in C# 7.2 because there was no way to express that combination before.

Q: What is the default accessibility of a class and of a class member?

A top-level class defaults to internal, and a member inside a class defaults to private. The class default surprises people writing a library, because their type compiles fine but consumers cannot see it. The member default is usually what you want anyway, so writing private on fields is a style choice rather than a behaviour change.

Q: How do you unit-test an internal class without making it public?

You add InternalsVisibleTo pointing at the test project, either as an assembly attribute or as an item in the .csproj. That lets the tests see internal types while keeping them out of the public API. The alternative — making the class public just so the tests can reach it — means you have permanently committed to supporting that type for external consumers, which is a real cost for a testing convenience.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Getting the two compound modifiers backwards. Most people guess that protected internal is restrictive because it has two limiting words in it. It is the opposite — it is the permissive one.
  • Forgetting classes default to internal. Your library type is invisible to consumers and the error message does not point at the missing public.
  • internal is not security. Reflection can reach it, and InternalsVisibleTo opens it. It is a tool for keeping your API surface small, not for protecting secrets.
  • Forgetting you can set accessibility per accessor. { get; private set; } is often exactly what you want and saves writing a backing field by hand.

docs.title: 1.5 — static
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.4 Access modifiers · Next: 1.6 const, readonly, init, required

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• static means "this belongs to the type itself, not to any one object." There is exactly one of it, shared by everything, for as long as the program runs.
  • Static data that can change is the number one cause of two problems: memory leaks, and code you cannot test.
  • A static constructor runs once, automatically, just before the type is first used. The runtime makes sure it is safe when several threads hit it at the same time.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Normally, when you create an object, that object gets its own copy of every field. Ten objects, ten copies.

static breaks that rule. A static field has one copy, shared by every object of that type — and it exists even if you never create a single object.

A useful picture: think of a class as a blueprint for a house.

  • A normal field is like "how many bedrooms does this house have" — every house has its own answer.
  • A static field is like "how many houses have we built from this blueprint" — there is only one such number, and it belongs to the blueprint, not to any house.

That is the entire mechanism. The interesting part, and what interviews actually dig into, is what goes wrong because of it.

docs.title: Static fields and methods
docs.text:
public class Counter
{
    private static int _total;   // ONE of these, shared by all Counters
    private int _mine;           // each Counter gets its own

    public Counter()
    {
        _total++;   // goes up every single time anyone creates a Counter
        _mine++;    // always ends up as 1 for each object
    }
}

new Counter();
new Counter();
new Counter();
// _total is now 3.
// Each object's _mine is 1.

A static method can only touch static data directly. That is because there is no specific object for it to work on — there is no this.

docs.title: Static classes
docs.text:
A static class cannot be created with new, cannot be inherited from, and every member inside it must be static. The compiler enforces all of this.

You use it for pure helper functions — things that take input, return output, and remember nothing in between. Math, Console and File are all static classes.

public static class TemperatureConverter
{
    public static double ToFahrenheit(double celsius) => celsius * 9 / 5 + 32;
}

// Called on the type, never on an object:
var f = TemperatureConverter.ToFahrenheit(20);

docs.title: Static constructors
docs.text:
A static constructor sets up static data. It looks like a normal constructor but with no access modifier and no parameters:

public class Config
{
    public static readonly string Version;

    static Config()          // note: no 'public', no parameters
    {
        Version = LoadVersion();
    }
}

The rules that get asked about:

  • It runs once per program run, never again.
  • It runs automatically, just before the first time anything touches the type — either creating an object or reading a static member.
  • You cannot call it, and you cannot control exactly when it runs. You only get the guarantee that it happens before first use.
  • The runtime makes it thread-safe. If two threads touch the type at the same moment, one runs the constructor while the other waits.

And here is the dangerous part. If a static constructor throws an exception, the type is permanently broken for the rest of the program. Every later attempt to use it throws a TypeInitializationException — including the very first one. Even worse, the real error is hidden one level down inside InnerException, so the message you see does not tell you what actually happened.

The practical lesson: keep static constructors boring. No file reading, no network calls, no configuration loading — nothing that can fail.

docs.title: Static local functions
docs.text:
A local function is a small function declared inside another method. Adding static to it stops it from using variables from the method around it:

int Compute(int x)
{
    int notAllowed = 10;

    return Helper(x);

    static int Helper(int n) => n * 2;
    // Because this is 'static', it CANNOT touch 'notAllowed'.
    // If you try, the compiler stops you.
}

Why bother? Two reasons. It makes it obvious that the helper does not depend on anything around it. And it avoids allocating a hidden object to carry those captured variables — see 1.13. It is a small, free win, so it is worth making static your default for local functions.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Here is a good use and a bad use, side by side.

// GOOD: no data stored, just a calculation
public static class Slug
{
    public static string From(string title) =>
        string.Join('-', title.ToLowerInvariant().Split(' '));
}

// DANGEROUS: static data that changes
public static class Cache
{
    private static readonly Dictionary<string, User> _users = new();

    public static void Add(User u) => _users[u.Id] = u;
}

That second one has three separate problems. Being able to list them all is a very good answer if an interviewer shows you code like this:

  1. It is not thread-safe. A plain Dictionary cannot handle two threads writing at once. In a web application, requests run at the same time, so this will eventually corrupt the dictionary or hang a thread in an infinite loop.
  2. Nothing is ever removed. It only grows. That is a memory leak by design — the program will slowly eat memory until it dies.
  3. It breaks when you run more than one server. Each server gets its own copy, so a user might see fresh data on one request and stale data on the next, depending on which machine answered.

The fixes, in order of how far you have scaled: ConcurrentDictionary for thread safety, then IMemoryCache for automatic eviction (see 19.2), then a distributed cache like Redis once you run multiple servers (see 19.3).

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a static constructor and when does it run?

It is a constructor that sets up static data. It takes no parameters and no access modifier, and you never call it yourself. The runtime runs it automatically, exactly once, just before the first time anything touches that type — whether that is creating an object or reading a static field. The runtime also guarantees it is thread-safe, so if two threads reach the type at the same moment, one runs it and the other waits.

Q: What happens if a static constructor throws an exception?

The type becomes permanently unusable for the rest of the program. The exception gets wrapped in a TypeInitializationException, and every later attempt to touch the type throws the same thing again. It is painful to diagnose, because the useful information is buried in InnerException and because the failure often shows up far away from the code that caused it. That is why static constructors should never do anything that can fail — no I/O, no configuration reading.

Q: Why is static state a problem in an ASP.NET Core application?

Three reasons. It is shared across every request, and requests run concurrently, so any static data that changes needs proper thread safety. It lives for the whole life of the process, so anything it holds on to can never be garbage collected — that is a very common source of memory leaks. And you cannot replace it in a test, so any class that depends on it becomes hard to test on its own. Dependency injection with a singleton lifetime gives you the same "one shared instance" behaviour without any of those three problems.

Q: What does static do on a local function?

It stops the function from using variables from the method around it. That means the compiler does not have to create a hidden object to hold those variables, so you avoid an allocation. It also makes the function easier to reason about, because you can see at a glance that it only depends on its own parameters. It is worth defaulting to static whenever the local function does not need anything from outside.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Static fields are shared across threads. In a web app that means shared across requests happening at the same time. Anything static that can change needs a lock or a thread-safe type.
  • Anything a static field points to can never be garbage collected. A static List that only ever gets added to is a guaranteed leak. See 3.5.
  • Static makes code hard to test. You cannot swap a static call for a fake one. This is exactly why DateTime.Now scattered through a codebase makes time-based logic untestable — and why TimeProvider was added. See 20.12.
  • An exception in a static constructor kills the type forever, and hides the real error inside InnerException.
  • A static class is not the same as a singleton. A singleton is a normal object that happens to be created once. It can implement interfaces, be injected, and be replaced in tests. A static class can do none of those. Prefer a DI singleton — see 6.3.

docs.title: 1.6 — const vs readonly vs init vs required
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.5 static · Next: 1.7 Inheritance

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• const is decided when you compile, and the value gets copied into every project that uses it. That copying is the trap.
  • readonly is decided when the program runs. You set it in the declaration or in the constructor, then it is locked.
  • init lets you set a property only while creating the object. required forces the caller to set it at all.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
All four of these mean some version of "you cannot change this". The difference is when the value gets locked in:

Keyword Locked in at const Compile time — before the program ever runs readonly End of the constructor init End of object creation required (Does not lock anything — it forces the caller to provide a value)

The const copying issue is the real reason this question gets asked. It causes a bug that is genuinely baffling if you have not seen it before.

docs.title: const — frozen at compile time
docs.text:
The value must be something the compiler can work out on its own. It is automatically static. You can only use it for simple built-in types: numbers, bool, char, string, and null.

public const int MaxRetries = 3;
public const string ApiVersion = "v1";

public const DateTime Epoch = new DateTime(1970, 1, 1);
// ERROR. Creating a DateTime requires running code,
// and the compiler cannot run code. Use static readonly instead.

Now the trap. When you use a const from another project, the compiler does not look it up at runtime. It copies the actual value into your compiled code.

Here is what that means in practice:

  1. Your library PaymentLib has public const int MaxRetries = 3;
  2. Your app references PaymentLib and uses MaxRetries.
  3. The compiler writes the literal number 3 into your app's compiled file.
  4. You ship a new PaymentLib where MaxRetries = 5.
  5. You drop the new DLL in without recompiling the app.
  6. Your app still uses 3. The new value is completely ignored.

This is very hard to debug, because you can open the library, see 5, and watch the app behave as if it were 3.

The rule: use const only for values that will never change — mathematical constants, fixed protocol numbers, things you would be happy carving into stone. For anything else that is public, use static readonly. It looks exactly the same to whoever is using it, but it is read at runtime, so an updated library takes effect immediately.

docs.title: readonly — frozen after the constructor
docs.text:
You can assign it in two places: where you declare it, or inside a constructor. Nowhere else. It is evaluated while the program runs, so any expression is allowed.

public class Service
{
    private readonly IRepository _repo;                          // set in constructor
    private static readonly DateTime Started = DateTime.UtcNow;  // set at first use

    public Service(IRepository repo) => _repo = repo;
}

The second trap: readonly protects the variable, not the object it points to.

private readonly List<string> _items = new();

_items = new List<string>();
// ERROR — you cannot point the field at a different list.

_items.Add("this is completely allowed");
// FINE — the list itself is still a normal, changeable list.

Going back to the analogy from 1.1: readonly means you cannot rub out the address written on the paper. It does nothing to stop anyone walking into the house and rearranging the furniture.

For real protection you need a type that genuinely cannot change. Expose it as IReadOnlyList<T> so callers cannot see Add, or use ImmutableArray<T> if you want it enforced properly.

docs.title: init — set it while creating the object, then never again
docs.text:
Introduced in C# 9. An init property can be assigned in an object initialiser (the { ... } block when you use new) or in a constructor, and after that it is locked.

public class Person
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
}

var p = new Person { Name = "Ada" };   // Allowed — we are still creating it
p.Name = "Grace";                      // ERROR — creation is finished

Before init existed, you had to choose between two bad options: a constructor with a long list of parameters, or a class where everything stays changeable forever. init gives you the readable { Name = ... } syntax and immutability.

docs.title: required — the caller must supply it
docs.text:
Introduced in C# 11. This one is different from the other three: it does not control whether something can change, it controls whether the caller is allowed to leave it out.

public class Person
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }   // must be given, then locked
    public string? Nickname { get; init; }       // optional
}

var a = new Person { Name = "Ada" };   // Fine
var b = new Person();                  // COMPILE ERROR: you did not set Name

Notice that last line fails at compile time, not at runtime. That is the whole value: "you forgot to set Name" changes from a null reference exception in production into a red squiggle in your editor.

required plus init together give you the safety of a constructor with the readability of an object initialiser.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
public class OrderProcessor
{
    // This genuinely never changes. const is fine.
    private const int MaxLineItems = 100;

    // This might change in a future version, and it is public.
    // static readonly, so consumers pick up the new value without recompiling.
    public static readonly TimeSpan DefaultTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);

    // Injected once at construction and never replaced.
    private readonly IPaymentGateway _gateway;

    public OrderProcessor(IPaymentGateway gateway) => _gateway = gateway;
}

public record CreateOrderRequest
{
    // Caller MUST provide these. Compile error if they forget.
    public required Guid CustomerId { get; init; }
    public required IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines { get; init; }

    // Genuinely optional
    public string? PromoCode { get; init; }
}

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between const and readonly?

const is worked out at compile time, is automatically static, and only works for simple built-in types like numbers and strings. readonly is worked out at runtime and can be assigned either where it is declared or inside a constructor, so it can hold any type and any computed value. The important practical difference is that const values get copied into every project that uses them. So if you change a public const in a library, every application using it keeps the old value until it is recompiled. That makes static readonly much safer for anything public that might ever change.

Q: Does readonly make an object immutable?

No. It makes the field unassignable — you cannot point it at a different object. If the field holds something changeable like a List, you can still add and remove items freely. For genuine immutability the type itself has to be immutable, so you would expose it as IReadOnlyList<T> or use something like ImmutableArray<T>.

Q: What does init give you that a constructor does not?

Object initialiser syntax. Before init, making a class immutable meant writing a constructor, and a class with ten mostly-optional properties meant either a huge parameter list or a builder class. With init you can set properties by name, in any order, leaving out the ones you do not need — and the property is still locked afterwards. Add required and the compiler also checks you did not forget the mandatory ones, so you get the safety of a constructor with the readability of an initialiser.

Q: When would you use required?

For any property the object cannot be valid without, when you do not want to write a constructor. It is especially good for DTOs and configuration classes that have a mix of mandatory and optional properties. The benefit is that forgetting one becomes a compile error instead of a null reference exception somewhere later.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Changing a public const in a library is a breaking change that does not look like one. Consumers keep the old value until they recompile. Use static readonly for public values that could ever change.
  • readonly on a field holding an object does not freeze the object. Only the field.
  • const cannot hold a DateTime, TimeSpan, or anything built with new. Those need static readonly.
  • readonly can still be changed by reflection. It is a compile-time promise, not a runtime lock.
  • required is not validation. It is checked when your code creates the object. A JSON deserializer or an ORM that builds objects a different way can still leave it unset. For real input validation use proper validation attributes — see 11.4.
