docs.title: 1.7 — Inheritance: virtual, override, new, sealed, abstract
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.6 const, readonly, init, required · Next: 1.8 Interfaces

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• virtual + override = the real object decides which method runs.
  • new = the variable's declared type decides which method runs. This is almost always a bug, and it is the most-asked trap in this topic.
  • A class can inherit from only one class, but can implement many interfaces. sealed stops anyone inheriting further.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Inheritance lets one class build on another, reusing its code and changing parts of it.

Almost all the interview value here sits in one distinction: overriding versus hiding. If you understand that clearly, you have covered most of what gets asked.

Two words first:

  • Base class — the class being inherited from. Also called the parent.
  • Derived class — the class doing the inheriting. Also called the child or subclass.

docs.title: virtual and override — the real object wins
docs.text:
virtual on a method means "a derived class is allowed to replace this". override means "here is my replacement".

The important part: C# decides which version to run by looking at what the object actually is, not what type the variable says it is.

public class Animal
{
    public virtual string Speak() => "...";
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override string Speak() => "Woof";
}

Animal a = new Dog();
// The VARIABLE says Animal.
// The OBJECT is actually a Dog.

a.Speak();   // "Woof"
// The object wins. This is polymorphism.

This is what makes inheritance useful. You can write code that works with Animal and it will automatically do the right thing for every kind of animal you create later.

docs.title: new — the variable wins (the trap)
docs.text:
new does something completely different. It does not replace the base method. It creates a separate, unrelated method that just happens to share the name.

And this time C# decides which one to run by looking at the declared type of the variable.

public class Cat : Animal
{
    public new string Speak() => "Meow";   // 'new', not 'override'
}

Now watch the same object give two different answers:

Animal a = new Cat();
a.Speak();   // "..." — the BASE method!
// The variable is declared as Animal, so C# runs Animal's version.
// It does not care that the object is really a Cat.

Cat c = new Cat();
c.Speak();   // "Meow"
// Same kind of object. Different declared type. Different answer.

One object, two answers, depending only on how you declared the variable. That is the demonstration to have ready in an interview.

If you leave out the word new when hiding, you only get a warning, not an error. So this can happen by accident.

Practical advice: if you find yourself writing new on a method, stop. Nine times out of ten you meant override and forgot to put virtual on the base method.

So why does new exist at all? For a specific problem: imagine you write class MyList that inherits from someone else's library class, and you add a method called Sort. Later, the library authors add their own Sort. Without new, your code would suddenly break. new lets you say "I know there is a clash, mine is separate, leave me alone."

docs.title: abstract — incomplete on purpose
docs.text:
abstract on a class means you cannot create it directly. It only exists to be inherited from.

abstract on a method means it has no body, and every derived class must provide one.

public abstract class Shape
{
    // No body. Every shape must supply its own.
    public abstract double Area();

    // A normal method with a body — every shape gets this for free.
    public string Describe() => $"Area: {Area():F2}";
}

var s = new Shape();   // ERROR — Shape is abstract, it is incomplete

Notice how Describe calls Area even though Area has no implementation here. That works because by the time the code actually runs, the object is always some real shape that has filled Area in.

That combination — some methods finished, some left for the child to fill in — is the main advantage an abstract class has over an interface.

docs.title: sealed — no more inheriting
docs.text:
public sealed class FinalDog : Animal { }
// Nothing can inherit from FinalDog. The chain stops here.

public class Puppy : Dog
{
    public sealed override string Speak() => "Yip";
    // Puppy CAN be inherited from,
    // but no further class may override Speak() again.
}

There are two reasons to seal a class.

The design reason: you are saying "I did not design this to be extended". That protects you from a real problem where someone inherits from your class, depends on some internal detail of how it works, and then your next update breaks their code.

The performance reason: when the compiler knows nothing can override a method, it can call it directly instead of looking it up at runtime, and sometimes copy the method body straight into the caller. That is a small but free speed-up on frequently used types.

docs.title: base — reaching the parent
docs.text:
public class Dog : Animal
{
    public Dog(string name) : base(name) { }
    // Calls Animal's constructor first, passing the name up

    public override string Speak() => base.Speak() + " Woof";
    // Runs Animal's version, then adds to it
}

Constructors run parent first, then child. And that creates a trap.

If a base constructor calls a virtual method, the derived class's override runs — but at that moment the derived constructor has not run yet. So the derived object's fields are still empty:

public class Base
{
    public Base() => Init();                    // runs FIRST
    protected virtual void Init() { }
}

public class Derived : Base
{
    private readonly List<int> _items = new();  // runs AFTER Base's constructor

    protected override void Init() => _items.Add(1);
    // CRASH! _items is still null right now.
}

Never call virtual methods from a constructor. The null reference this produces looks impossible when you are debugging it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Here is a realistic example — a shared payment flow where each provider fills in one step.

public abstract class PaymentProcessor
{
    // The shared recipe. Every processor follows these three steps in this order.
    public async Task<Receipt> ProcessAsync(Payment p, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        Validate(p);                                 // step 1 — can be customised
        var result = await ChargeAsync(p, ct);       // step 2 — MUST be supplied
        return BuildReceipt(result);                 // step 3 — always the same
    }

    // virtual: there is a sensible default, but children may add to it
    protected virtual void Validate(Payment p)
    {
        if (p.Amount <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
    }

    // abstract: there is no sensible default. Every child MUST write this.
    protected abstract Task<ChargeResult> ChargeAsync(Payment p, CancellationToken ct);

    // private: nobody can change this. It is the same for everyone.
    private Receipt BuildReceipt(ChargeResult r) => new(r.TransactionId, r.Amount);
}

And a concrete implementation:

public sealed class StripeProcessor(IStripeClient client) : PaymentProcessor
{
    // Required — the base class declared this abstract
    protected override Task<ChargeResult> ChargeAsync(Payment p, CancellationToken ct)
        => client.ChargeAsync(p.Amount, p.Currency, ct);

    // Optional — we are adding an extra rule on top of the default one
    protected override void Validate(Payment p)
    {
        base.Validate(p);   // don't lose the base rule! Easy to forget.

        if (p.Currency is not ("USD" or "EUR"))
            throw new NotSupportedException($"Unsupported currency {p.Currency}");
    }
}

Two things to notice:

  • ProcessAsync is not virtual. The order of the steps is fixed. Only the individual steps can vary. This is called the Template Method pattern — see 22.5.
  • base.Validate(p) has to be written explicitly. If you forget it, you silently lose the "amount must be positive" check.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between override and new?

override replaces the base method, and C# decides which version to run based on what the object actually is at runtime. new does not replace anything — it declares a separate method that happens to share the name, and C# decides which to run based on the declared type of the variable. So with new, the same object gives you the base method when called through a base-typed variable and the derived method through a derived-typed variable — two different answers for one object. That is almost always a bug. new mainly exists so that a base class adding a new method later does not silently break classes that already inherit from it.

Q: When would you use an abstract class instead of an interface?

An abstract class when there is real shared code or shared state to inherit, and when the types genuinely form an "is-a" relationship — a StripeProcessor is a PaymentProcessor. An interface when you are describing a capability that unrelated types can have, or when a type needs to satisfy several contracts, because C# only allows one base class. In practice I usually define the contract as an interface so consumers depend on that, and add an abstract base class only when there is genuinely shared implementation. That way the base class is an implementation detail rather than part of the public design.

Q: Why would you seal a class?

Two reasons. Design: you are stating that this class was not built to be inherited from, which avoids the problem where someone's subclass quietly depends on internal behaviour that you then change. Performance: because the compiler knows no one can override the methods, it can call them directly rather than looking them up, and sometimes inline them. It is a reasonable default for concrete classes you did not deliberately design for extension.

Q: Can you call a virtual method from a constructor?

You can, but you should not. Constructors run from the base class down, so a virtual call in a base constructor jumps into the derived override at a point where the derived constructor has not run yet. All the derived class's fields are still null or zero, and its readonly fields are unassigned. The result is a null reference exception that looks impossible when you read the code, because the field it complains about is clearly initialised right there in the class.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Writing new when you meant override. Which method runs then depends on the variable's declared type, and it only produces a warning if you leave the keyword off.
  • Calling virtual methods from a constructor. The override runs before the derived class has set up its own fields.
  • Forgetting base.Method() inside an override. The base version does not run automatically. If it did something important, you have just silently removed it.
  • C# has no multiple class inheritance. One base class only. Any number of interfaces.
  • Deep inheritance chains are a warning sign. Past two or three levels, it becomes very hard to work out where behaviour actually comes from. Composition is usually clearer — see 22.2.
  • protected members are part of your public API. Anyone inheriting from your class depends on them, so changing one is a breaking change even though it is not public.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An interface is a contract. It lists what a type can do, without saying how.
  • A class can implement many interfaces but inherit from only one class. That is often the deciding factor.
  • Interfaces are what make dependency injection and unit testing possible — you depend on the contract, and swap the real thing for a fake one in tests.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An interface is a list of promises. It says "any type claiming to be this must provide these members" — but it does not say how.

A good real-world comparison is a wall socket. The socket is the interface. It promises a certain shape and a certain voltage. A lamp, a laptop charger and a kettle all plug into the same socket, and the socket does not know or care what they do with the electricity. You can unplug one and plug in another, and the wall does not change.

That is exactly why interfaces matter in real applications. Your code plugs into IEmailSender. In production you plug in the real one that talks to SendGrid. In tests you plug in a fake one that just records what was sent. Your code never changes.

docs.title: Declaring and implementing
docs.text:
public interface IEmailSender
{
    Task SendAsync(string to, string subject, string body);
}

public class SendGridEmailSender : IEmailSender
{
    public Task SendAsync(string to, string subject, string body)
    {
        // real implementation
    }
}

Notice the interface has no body for the method — just the signature and a semicolon. Interface members are automatically public; you cannot and should not write public in front of them.

docs.title: One class, many interfaces
docs.text:
This is the key structural difference from inheritance:

public class FileLogger : ILogger, IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable
{
    // must implement all members of all three
}

A class can only have one base class, but it can promise as many contracts as it likes. When you need a type to fit into several different systems, interfaces are the only option.

docs.title: Explicit implementation
docs.text:
Sometimes two interfaces declare a member with the same name, or you want a member available only when the object is used through a specific interface. You can implement it explicitly by prefixing the interface name:

public interface IFileReader { string Read(); }
public interface IDatabaseReader { string Read(); }

public class DataSource : IFileReader, IDatabaseReader
{
    // Two methods with the same name — distinguished by which interface
    string IFileReader.Read() => "from file";
    string IDatabaseReader.Read() => "from database";
}

Now watch how you have to call them:

var ds = new DataSource();

ds.Read();
// ERROR — DataSource itself has no public Read method.
// Explicitly implemented members are hidden from the class's own surface.

((IFileReader)ds).Read();       // "from file"
((IDatabaseReader)ds).Read();   // "from database"

IFileReader reader = ds;
reader.Read();                  // "from file" — cleaner way to write it

Explicit implementation is also used to hide a member you must implement but do not want people calling casually — IDisposable.Dispose on a type where disposal should happen a different way, for example.

docs.title: Default interface methods (C# 8+)
docs.text:
Since C# 8, an interface can provide a body for a method:

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log(string message);

    // A default. Implementers get this free unless they replace it.
    void LogError(Exception ex) => Log($"ERROR: {ex.Message}");
}

This was added mainly so library authors can add a method to an existing interface without breaking everyone who already implements it. Before C# 8, adding a member to a published interface broke every implementer immediately.

It is not meant as a replacement for abstract classes. Interfaces still cannot hold state (no fields), so anything needing shared data still wants a class.

One thing to be careful about: default methods are only visible through the interface, not through the class:

public class ConsoleLogger : ILogger
{
    public void Log(string m) => Console.WriteLine(m);
    // LogError not implemented — we use the default
}

var logger = new ConsoleLogger();
logger.LogError(ex);              // ERROR — not on the class

ILogger asInterface = logger;
asInterface.LogError(ex);         // works

docs.title: Interface vs abstract class
docs.text:
Interface Abstract class How many can a class have? Many One Can hold fields / state? No Yes Can have constructors? No Yes Can have implemented methods? Yes, since C# 8 (defaults) Yes, always Access modifiers on members? Always public Any Relationship it expresses "can do this" "is a kind of this"

The practical rule: define the contract as an interface so consumers depend on that. Add an abstract base class only if there is genuinely shared code. That way the base class stays an implementation detail rather than part of your public design.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Here is why interfaces matter in ASP.NET Core specifically.

// The contract
public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task SaveAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct);
}

// Your business logic depends on the CONTRACT, never on the real database class
public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo, IEmailSender email)
{
    public async Task CompleteAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.GetAsync(id, ct)
                    ?? throw new NotFoundException(id);

        order.Complete();
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Order complete", "Thanks!");
    }
}

In production you register the real implementations:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailSender, SendGridEmailSender>();

In a unit test you pass in fakes instead:

[Fact]
public async Task CompleteAsync_SendsConfirmationEmail()
{
    var repo = Substitute.For<IOrderRepository>();
    var email = Substitute.For<IEmailSender>();
    repo.GetAsync(id, default).Returns(new Order(id));

    var service = new OrderService(repo, email);
    await service.CompleteAsync(id, default);

    await email.Received(1).SendAsync(Arg.Any<string>(), "Order complete", Arg.Any<string>());
}

This test touches no database and sends no email. It runs in milliseconds. That is only possible because OrderService asked for interfaces rather than concrete classes. This is the single most practical reason interviewers care about interfaces.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an interface and why would you use one?

An interface is a contract that lists what members a type must have, without saying how they work. You use it so that code can depend on what something does rather than how it does it. That gives you two big wins. You can swap implementations without changing the consuming code — the same service can work against SQL Server in production and an in-memory fake in tests. And it lets a class satisfy several contracts at once, which you cannot do with inheritance because C# only allows one base class.

Q: Interface or abstract class — how do you choose?

I ask whether there is shared implementation. If the types genuinely share code and state, and they form a real "is-a" family, an abstract class is right — it can hold fields, have a constructor, and provide finished methods. If I am describing a capability that unrelated types might have, or if the type already needs a different base class, it has to be an interface. In practice I lean towards an interface for the public contract and only add an abstract base class underneath when there is real duplication to remove.

Q: What are default interface methods and why were they added?

Since C# 8, an interface member can have a body, which implementing types inherit unless they override it. The main reason they were added was versioning — before this, adding a method to a published interface broke every single class implementing it. Now a library can add a method with a default body and existing implementers keep compiling. They are not a replacement for abstract classes, because interfaces still cannot hold state.

Q: What is explicit interface implementation?

It is when you implement a member by writing the interface name in front of it, like string IFileReader.Read(). The member then only exists when the object is accessed through that interface — it is not part of the class's own public surface. You need it when two interfaces declare members with the same signature and you want them to behave differently, or when you have to implement something but do not want to encourage people to call it directly on the class.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Explicitly implemented members are invisible on the class. You must cast to the interface, or assign to an interface-typed variable, to call them.
  • Default interface methods are also only visible through the interface, not through the class that implements it. This surprises people.
  • Interfaces cannot hold state. No fields. If your "interface" needs data, it wants to be an abstract class.
  • An interface with one implementation and no test double is often unnecessary. Do not create an interface for every class out of habit — that is ceremony without benefit. Add it when you actually need to substitute, mock, or support multiple implementations.
  • Adding a member to a published interface is a breaking change unless you give it a default body.
  • Interface members are always public. Writing public in front is a compile error, and you cannot make one private or protected.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Polymorphism means one name, many behaviours.
  • Compile-time polymorphism = method overloading. The compiler picks based on the arguments you passed.
  • Runtime polymorphism = method overriding. The runtime picks based on what the object actually is.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
The word comes from Greek: poly = many, morph = shape. "Many shapes."

In practice it means you can write one piece of code that works correctly with many different types, without knowing in advance which one it will get.

A simple picture: think of the word "draw". You can draw a circle, draw a square, draw a triangle. Same instruction, different result depending on what you are drawing. You do not need a separate word for each shape.

C# gives you two flavours, and interviewers usually want you to name both.

docs.title: Compile-time polymorphism (overloading)
docs.text:
Several methods share a name but take different parameters. The compiler works out which one you meant by looking at the arguments at the call site.

public class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;
    public double Add(double a, double b) => a + b;
    public int Add(int a, int b, int c) => a + b + c;
}

calc.Add(1, 2);        // picks the first — two ints
calc.Add(1.5, 2.5);    // picks the second — two doubles
calc.Add(1, 2, 3);     // picks the third — three ints

This is decided before the program ever runs. By the time the code executes, the decision is already baked in. That is why it is called compile-time (or "static") polymorphism.

What counts as a different overload: the number of parameters, their types, or their order.

What does NOT count: the return type. This is a common exam-style question:

public int GetValue() => 1;
public string GetValue() => "1";
// ERROR. You cannot overload on return type alone.

The reason is simple — if you write GetValue(); on its own line and ignore the result, the compiler would have no way to know which one you meant.

Operator overloading is also compile-time polymorphism. See 1.19.

docs.title: Runtime polymorphism (overriding)
docs.text:
This is the more important kind. A base class declares a virtual method, derived classes override it, and the runtime picks the right version based on what the object actually is.

public abstract class Shape
{
    public abstract double Area();
}

public class Circle(double radius) : Shape
{
    public override double Area() => Math.PI * radius * radius;
}

public class Rectangle(double w, double h) : Shape
{
    public override double Area() => w * h;
}

Now the payoff:

List<Shape> shapes =
[
    new Circle(1),
    new Rectangle(2, 3),
    new Circle(5)
];

double total = shapes.Sum(s => s.Area());
// Each s.Area() call runs the RIGHT version automatically.
// This loop has no idea circles or rectangles exist.

Look at that last line closely. The code says s.Area() where s is just a Shape. It does not check the type. It does not have an if or a switch. Yet each object runs its own correct calculation.

And this is the real benefit: if you add a Triangle class tomorrow, this loop keeps working with no changes at all. That is polymorphism paying for itself.

Compare with what you would otherwise write:

// The version WITHOUT polymorphism — every new shape means editing this
double total = 0;
foreach (var s in shapes)
{
    if (s is Circle c) total += Math.PI * c.Radius * c.Radius;
    else if (s is Rectangle r) total += r.Width * r.Height;
    // ...and you must remember to come back here for every new shape
}

A long chain of type checks like this is a strong hint that polymorphism is the better answer. This is also what the open/closed principle in SOLID is about — see 22.1.

docs.title: Interfaces give you polymorphism too
docs.text:
You do not need inheritance. An interface works just as well:

public interface IPaymentMethod { Task PayAsync(decimal amount); }

public class CreditCard : IPaymentMethod { /* ... */ }
public class PayPal     : IPaymentMethod { /* ... */ }

// Works with any payment method, present or future
async Task Checkout(IPaymentMethod method, decimal amount)
    => await method.PayAsync(amount);

This is usually the preferred approach in modern C#, because it does not force your types into an inheritance hierarchy.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Putting both kinds together:

public abstract class Notifier
{
    // Runtime polymorphism — each subclass sends differently
    public abstract Task SendAsync(string recipient, string message);

    // Compile-time polymorphism — three convenient ways to call it
    public Task SendAsync(User user, string message)
        => SendAsync(user.Email, message);

    public Task SendAsync(IEnumerable<User> users, string message)
        => Task.WhenAll(users.Select(u => SendAsync(u, message)));
}

public class EmailNotifier(IEmailSender sender) : Notifier
{
    public override Task SendAsync(string recipient, string message)
        => sender.SendAsync(recipient, "Notification", message);
}

public class SmsNotifier(ISmsGateway gateway) : Notifier
{
    public override Task SendAsync(string recipient, string message)
        => gateway.SendTextAsync(recipient, message);
}

Now calling code just holds a Notifier and calls SendAsync. It does not know or care whether an email or a text message goes out.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is polymorphism?

It means one name can behave in different ways depending on the context. C# has two forms. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading — several methods share a name but take different parameters, and the compiler picks the right one from the arguments. Runtime polymorphism is method overriding — a base class declares a virtual method, derived classes override it, and the runtime picks the version matching the actual object. The second one is the important one, because it lets you write code that works with types that did not exist when you wrote it.

Q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?

Overloading is several methods with the same name in the same class, differing by their parameters, resolved by the compiler before the program runs. Overriding is a derived class replacing a virtual method from its base class, resolved by the runtime based on the actual object. So overloading is about convenience at the call site, and overriding is about substituting behaviour.

Q: Can you overload a method by changing only the return type?

No. If you called the method and ignored its result, the compiler would have no information to decide which one you meant. Overloads have to differ by the number, types, or order of their parameters.

Q: How does polymorphism help in real code?

It lets you write code that works with future types. If I have a list of shapes and call Area() on each one, I never have to touch that loop again when someone adds a new shape. Without it, you end up with a growing chain of type checks that has to be updated in every place whenever a new type appears — and eventually someone forgets one. That is exactly what the open/closed principle is warning about.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• new does not give you polymorphism. It hides the base method, and which version runs depends on the variable's declared type, not the object. See 1.7.
  • A method must be virtual or abstract to be overridden. Marking it override in the derived class is not enough on its own.
  • Overload resolution can surprise you. When you pass a null, or a type that could convert to several parameter types, the compiler picks by rules that are not always obvious. Cast explicitly when it is ambiguous.
  • Long if (x is TypeA) ... else if (x is TypeB) chains usually mean polymorphism was the better design.
  • Polymorphism is not free at runtime. A virtual call costs a lookup. It is almost never worth worrying about, but it is why sealed can help in genuinely hot code.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Generics let you write code once and use it with any type, without giving up type safety and without boxing.
  • Constraints (where T : ...) tell the compiler what T is allowed to be, so you can actually do things with it.
  • Covariance (out) lets you use a more derived type where a base type is expected. Contravariance (in) is the opposite. Only interfaces and delegates support them.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Imagine you need a list of integers, a list of strings, and a list of orders. Without generics you have three bad options:

  1. Write IntList, StringList and OrderList by hand — the same code three times.
  2. Write one ObjectList that holds object — but then everything gets boxed (see 1.1), you lose type checking, and you have to cast everything back on the way out.
  3. Use generics.

Generics let you write the list once, with a placeholder for the type:

List<int>     numbers = new();
List<string>  names   = new();
List<Order>   orders  = new();

One implementation. Full type checking. No boxing. That combination is why generics exist.

Think of T as a blank space in a form. You write the form once, and each person fills in the blank differently.

docs.title: Generic classes and methods
docs.text:
public class Box<T>
{
    private T? _item;

    public void Put(T item) => _item = item;
    public T? Take() => _item;
}

var intBox = new Box<int>();
intBox.Put(42);
int value = intBox.Take();     // no cast needed — compiler knows it is an int

intBox.Put("hello");           // COMPILE ERROR — caught before you run

That last line is the point. With an object-based version, this would compile fine and then crash at runtime with an invalid cast. Generics move the error from runtime to compile time.

Generic methods work the same way, and the compiler can usually work out the type for you:

public static T? FirstOrDefault<T>(IEnumerable<T> items)
{
    foreach (var item in items) return item;
    return default;
}

var n = FirstOrDefault(new[] { 1, 2, 3 });
// You did not write FirstOrDefault<int>. The compiler
// worked out T = int from the argument. This is called type inference.

docs.title: Constraints — telling the compiler what T can do
docs.text:
By default the compiler knows almost nothing about T, so you can barely use it:

public T Largest<T>(T a, T b)
{
    return a > b ? a : b;
    // ERROR. The compiler does not know T supports '>'.
    // T could be anything, including a type with no comparison.
}

A constraint narrows what T is allowed to be, which lets the compiler allow more:

public T Largest<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
{
    return a.CompareTo(b) > 0 ? a : b;   // now this is fine
}

The constraints you should know:

Constraint Means where T : class must be a reference type where T : struct must be a value type where T : new() must have a public constructor with no parameters where T : SomeClass must be that class or inherit from it where T : ISomeInterface must implement that interface where T : notnull cannot be a nullable type where T : U must be, or inherit from, another type parameter

You can combine them, but the order is fixed: class/struct first, then base class, then interfaces, then new() last.

public class Repository<T> where T : Entity, IAuditable, new()
{
    public T Create() => new T();     // allowed because of new()
}

docs.title: Covariance and contravariance
docs.text:
This is the part people find hardest, so here it is slowly.

The question being answered is: if Dog is an Animal, is List<Dog> a List<Animal>?

The natural guess is yes. The correct answer is no, and here is why:

List<Animal> animals = new List<Dog>();   // Imagine this were allowed
animals.Add(new Cat());                   // Perfectly legal — Cat is an Animal
// But the actual list is a List<Dog>. We just put a Cat in it.

Allowing it would break type safety. So by default, generics are invariant — List<Dog> and List<Animal> are simply unrelated types.

But sometimes it is safe, and that is what out and in are for.

Covariance — out — safe when you only ever take things OUT.

public interface IEnumerable<out T> { /* ... */ }

IEnumerable<Animal> animals = new List<Dog>();   // ALLOWED

This is safe because IEnumerable<T> only lets you read. There is no Add. If you can only take dogs out and treat them as animals, nothing can go wrong.

Contravariance — in — safe when you only ever put things IN.

public interface IComparer<in T> { int Compare(T x, T y); }

IComparer<Dog> dogComparer = new AnimalComparer();   // ALLOWED

This looks backwards at first. Read it as: something that can compare any two animals is certainly capable of comparing two dogs. A more general tool can always do a more specific job.

A memory aid that works:

out = output = you take values out = covariant (more derived is fine). in = input = you put values in = contravariant (more general is fine).

Two important limitations: this only works on interfaces and delegates, never on classes. And it only works for reference types — IEnumerable<int> is not an IEnumerable<object>, because that would need boxing.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic generic repository, which is a very common interview example:

public interface IRepository<T> where T : class, IEntity
{
    Task<T?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ListAsync(CancellationToken ct);
    Task AddAsync(T entity, CancellationToken ct);
}

public class EfRepository<T>(AppDbContext db) : IRepository<T>
    where T : class, IEntity
{
    public Task<T?> GetAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
        => db.Set<T>().FirstOrDefaultAsync(e => e.Id == id, ct);

    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ListAsync(CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Set<T>().AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);

    public async Task AddAsync(T entity, CancellationToken ct)
        => await db.Set<T>().AddAsync(entity, ct);
}

Why the constraints are there:

  • class — because db.Set<T>() in EF Core requires a reference type.
  • IEntity — so we can rely on e.Id existing. Without it, e.Id would not compile.

Registering it in DI uses an open generic registration — one line covers every entity type:

builder.Services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));
// Now anyone can inject IRepository<Order>, IRepository<Customer>, etc.

See 6.8.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why do generics exist? What problem do they solve?

Before generics, a collection that could hold anything had to store object. That caused three problems. Value types got boxed, meaning a heap allocation for every number you stored. You lost type safety, so putting a string into what you thought was a list of numbers compiled fine and crashed later. And you had to cast everything on the way out, which is noisy and can fail. Generics solve all three at once — one implementation, checked at compile time, with no boxing.

Q: What are generic constraints and why do you need them?

A constraint tells the compiler what a type parameter is allowed to be, using where T : something. You need them because by default the compiler assumes T could be literally any type, so it will not let you do much with it — you cannot compare it, construct it, or call any method beyond what object provides. Adding where T : IComparable<T> lets you compare. Adding where T : new() lets you construct one. The constraint buys you capability.

Q: Explain covariance and contravariance.

By default generics are invariant — List<Dog> is not a List<Animal>, because if it were you could add a Cat to it through the base-typed reference and break type safety. Covariance, marked with out, allows the more derived version where the base is expected, and it is only safe when the type only ever produces values — which is why IEnumerable<T> has it and List<T> does not. Contravariance, marked with in, is the reverse: it allows a more general type where a specific one is expected, which is safe when the type only consumes values, like IComparer<T>. The memory aid is that out means output so covariant, in means input so contravariant. Both only work on interfaces and delegates, and only for reference types.

Q: Why does IEnumerable<int> not convert to IEnumerable<object>?

Because variance only works for reference types. Converting an int to an object requires boxing, which changes the actual representation in memory. Variance is built on the fact that a reference to a derived type is already a valid reference to the base type, with no conversion needed. That does not hold for value types.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Generics are invariant by default. List<Dog> is not a List<Animal> and never will be.
  • Variance only works on interfaces and delegates. You cannot put out or in on a class type parameter.
  • Variance does not work for value types. IEnumerable<int> is not an IEnumerable<object>.
  • default(T) is not always null. For a value type it is zero, for a bool it is false, for a struct it is a struct with all fields zeroed. Use default rather than null in generic code.
  • You cannot use most operators on an unconstrained T. No +, no >, no == in the way you expect. Static abstract interface members (C# 11) are the modern answer to generic maths.
  • Constraint order is fixed. class or struct first, then a base class, then interfaces, then new(). The compiler will reject any other order.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A delegate is a variable that holds a method. You can pass it around and call it later.
  • You almost never need to declare your own any more. Use the built-in ones: Action (returns nothing), Func (returns something), Predicate (returns bool).
  • A delegate can hold more than one method at once. That is called multicast, and it is how events work.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Normally a variable holds data — a number, a string, an object. A delegate holds a method.

Why is that useful? Because it lets you pass behaviour into a method, not just data.

A real-world picture: think of giving someone a phone number instead of an answer. You are not saying "the answer is 42". You are saying "when you need the answer, call this number". Whoever holds the number can call it whenever they like, and they do not need to know who picks up.

This is what makes LINQ, event handlers, and callbacks possible.

docs.title: The old way — declaring your own
docs.text:
// This declares a TYPE. It says: "a method that takes two ints
// and returns an int".
public delegate int MathOperation(int a, int b);

// Any method matching that shape can be stored in it
static int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;
static int Multiply(int a, int b) => a * b;

MathOperation op = Add;
int result = op(3, 4);     // 7 — this actually calls Add

op = Multiply;
result = op(3, 4);         // 12 — same variable, different method

Notice op = Add has no brackets. You are storing the method itself, not calling it. Adding brackets would call it and store the result instead.

docs.title: The modern way — built-in delegate types
docs.text:
You rarely declare your own delegate now. .NET provides generic ones that cover almost every shape:

Type Shape Example Action takes nothing, returns nothing Action greet = () => Console.WriteLine("hi"); Action<T> takes a T, returns nothing Action<string> log = m => Console.WriteLine(m); Action<T1,T2> takes two, returns nothing up to 16 parameters Func<TResult> takes nothing, returns a value Func<int> get = () => 42; Func<T,TResult> takes a T, returns a value Func<int,int> dbl = x => x * 2; Predicate<T> takes a T, returns bool Predicate<int> isEven = x => x % 2 == 0;

The rule for Func: the last type parameter is always the return type. So Func<int, string, bool> takes an int and a string, and returns a bool.

Predicate<T> is really just Func<T, bool> with a friendlier name. LINQ actually uses Func<T, bool>, not Predicate<T>.

So the earlier example becomes:

Func<int, int, int> op = Add;      // no custom delegate type needed

docs.title: Multicast — holding several methods
docs.text:
A delegate can hold a whole list of methods. Use += to add and -= to remove:

Action<string> pipeline = m => Console.WriteLine($"Console: {m}");
pipeline += m => File.AppendAllText("log.txt", m);
pipeline += m => telemetry.Track(m);

pipeline("Order created");
// Calls ALL THREE, in the order they were added.

Two things to be careful about with multicast delegates:

Only the last return value survives. If you multicast a Func, you get the result of the final method and every other result is silently thrown away. So multicasting only really makes sense for Action.

One exception stops everything after it. If the second method throws, the third never runs. If you need all of them to run regardless, you have to invoke them individually:

foreach (Action<string> handler in pipeline.GetInvocationList())
{
    try { handler(message); }
    catch (Exception ex) { logger.LogError(ex, "Handler failed"); }
}

docs.title: Where you already use delegates without noticing
docs.text:
Every LINQ method takes a delegate:

orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100)      // Func<Order, bool>
      .Select(o => o.CustomerName)     // Func<Order, string>
      .OrderBy(name => name)           // Func<string, string>

Each of those lambdas is a delegate being passed in. Where does not know what "expensive order" means — you tell it, by handing it a method.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Here is a realistic use: a retry helper that works with any operation.

public static async Task<T> RetryAsync<T>(
    Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>> operation,   // the work to do
    int maxAttempts,
    ILogger logger,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    for (var attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
    {
        try
        {
            return await operation(ct);           // call whatever we were given
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (attempt < maxAttempts)
        {
            logger.LogWarning(ex, "Attempt {Attempt} failed, retrying", attempt);
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(attempt), ct);
        }
    }
}

Used like this:

var order = await RetryAsync(
    ct => httpClient.GetFromJsonAsync<Order>("/orders/1", ct),
    maxAttempts: 3,
    logger,
    cancellationToken);

RetryAsync has no idea what it is retrying. It could be an HTTP call, a database query, or a file read. The delegate parameter is what makes it reusable — without it you would need a separate retry method for every kind of operation.

(In a real ASP.NET Core app you would use Polly for this rather than hand-rolling it — see 19.11. But the pattern is the same.)

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a delegate?

It is a type that holds a reference to a method, so you can store a method in a variable, pass it as an argument, and call it later. It is type-safe — the delegate's declaration specifies the parameters and return type, and the compiler checks that whatever you assign matches. Delegates are what make callbacks, event handlers, and LINQ possible, because they let you pass behaviour into a method rather than just data.

Q: What is the difference between Action, Func and Predicate?

They are all built-in generic delegate types. Action returns nothing — it is for methods you call for their side effects. Func returns a value, and the last type parameter is always the return type, so Func<int, string> takes an int and returns a string. Predicate<T> takes a T and returns a bool, so it is for tests and filters. In practice Predicate<T> is just a friendlier name for Func<T, bool>, and LINQ actually uses the Func form.

Q: What is a multicast delegate?

A delegate that holds more than one method. You add methods with += and remove them with -=, and invoking the delegate calls all of them in the order they were added. It is the mechanism behind events. Two things to watch: if the delegate returns a value you only get the last one, and if any handler throws, the ones after it never run. If you need every handler to run independently, you have to loop over GetInvocationList() and call them one at a time inside a try/catch.

Q: What is the difference between a delegate and an interface with one method?

They solve the same problem in different ways. An interface is better when the thing has identity and might grow more members, or when you want to inject it and mock it. A delegate is better for a single, simple, throwaway piece of behaviour — especially when you want to write it inline as a lambda. LINQ uses delegates because writing Where(o => o.Total > 100) inline is far nicer than declaring a class that implements IFilter<Order> every time.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• op = Add versus op = Add(). No brackets stores the method. Brackets calls it and stores the result. Easy typo, confusing error.
  • Multicast Func throws away all but the last return value, silently.
  • One throwing handler stops the rest. Use GetInvocationList() if that matters.
  • -= needs the exact same delegate instance to remove a lambda. Subscribing with x += () => Foo() and then unsubscribing with x -= () => Foo() does nothing at all — they are two different lambda objects. Store it in a variable first.
  • A delegate holding an instance method keeps that whole object alive. This is the main cause of event-related memory leaks — see 1.12.
  • Func<T,bool> and Predicate<T> are not interchangeable even though they look identical. They are different types, so you cannot pass one where the other is expected without conversion.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An event is a delegate with restrictions. Outsiders can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=). They cannot replace it or fire it.
  • The standard shape is EventHandler<TArgs>, and the standard way to raise it is MyEvent?.Invoke(this, args).
  • Forgetting to unsubscribe is a real memory leak. The publisher holds a reference to every subscriber, so subscribers never get collected.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An event is the "let me know when something happens" mechanism.

A newspaper subscription is the usual comparison, and it fits well. The newspaper (the publisher) does not know or care who its readers are. Readers (subscribers) sign up, receive every issue, and can cancel whenever they like. The newspaper just prints and sends.

In code: one object announces "something happened", and any number of other objects can have arranged to be told.

Events are built directly on delegates (1.11). An event is a multicast delegate wrapped in some protection.

docs.title: Why not just a public delegate?
docs.text:
You could use a plain public delegate field:

public class Order
{
    public Action<Order>? Completed;    // public delegate field — DON'T
}

But then anyone outside the class can do three things they should not be able to:

order.Completed = null;              // wipe out everyone else's subscriptions!
order.Completed = MyHandler;         // replace instead of add — same problem
order.Completed?.Invoke(order);      // fire the event from outside

Adding the event keyword blocks all three:

public class Order
{
    public event Action<Order>? Completed;    // now protected
}

From outside, only += and -= compile. Assignment and invocation are compile errors. Only code inside the declaring class can raise it. That is the entire purpose of the keyword.

docs.title: The standard pattern
docs.text:
.NET convention uses EventHandler<TEventArgs>, which is a delegate shaped as (object? sender, TEventArgs e):

public class OrderCompletedEventArgs(Guid orderId, decimal total) : EventArgs
{
    public Guid OrderId { get; } = orderId;
    public decimal Total { get; } = total;
}

public class OrderService
{
    public event EventHandler<OrderCompletedEventArgs>? OrderCompleted;

    public void Complete(Order order)
    {
        order.MarkComplete();

        // Raise it. The ?. is essential — see below.
        OrderCompleted?.Invoke(this, new OrderCompletedEventArgs(order.Id, order.Total));
    }
}

Subscribing:

var service = new OrderService();

service.OrderCompleted += (sender, e) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"Order {e.OrderId} completed for {e.Total:C}");

docs.title: Why ?.Invoke and not just Invoke
docs.text:
If nobody has subscribed, the event field is null. Calling Invoke on it throws a NullReferenceException.

The ?. handles that. But there is a subtler reason it is the recommended form: it also avoids a race condition. Consider the naive version:

if (OrderCompleted != null)
    OrderCompleted(this, args);
// If another thread unsubscribes the last handler BETWEEN these two lines,
// the second line throws even though we just checked.

?.Invoke reads the delegate into a temporary once and then calls it, so the check and the call happen on the same value. Since the delegate list itself cannot change once captured, this is safe.

docs.title: The memory leak ⚠️
docs.text:
This is the part interviewers care about most, so it is worth understanding properly.

When you subscribe, the publisher stores a reference to the subscriber.

public class OrderService          // long-lived — lives for the whole app
{
    public event EventHandler<OrderCompletedEventArgs>? OrderCompleted;
}

public class OrderPage             // short-lived — one per page view
{
    public OrderPage(OrderService service)
    {
        service.OrderCompleted += OnCompleted;    // subscribe
    }

    private void OnCompleted(object? s, OrderCompletedEventArgs e) { /* ... */ }
}

Now trace what happens:

  1. OrderPage subscribes. OrderService now holds a delegate.
  2. That delegate points at the OnCompleted method on that specific OrderPage object.
  3. So OrderService is holding a reference to the OrderPage.
  4. The user closes the page. Your code drops its reference to OrderPage.
  5. But OrderService is still holding one. The garbage collector cannot collect it.
  6. Repeat a thousand times. You now have a thousand dead pages in memory, all still receiving events.

This is a genuine memory leak, and it is the classic one in .NET.

The fix is to unsubscribe:

public class OrderPage : IDisposable
{
    private readonly OrderService _service;

    public OrderPage(OrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
        _service.OrderCompleted += OnCompleted;
    }

    public void Dispose()
    {
        _service.OrderCompleted -= OnCompleted;    // essential
    }
}

And a trap inside the trap: you cannot unsubscribe a lambda this way.

service.OrderCompleted += (s, e) => DoSomething();
service.OrderCompleted -= (s, e) => DoSomething();
// Does NOTHING. These are two different lambda objects
// that happen to contain the same code.

To unsubscribe a lambda you must keep a reference to it:

EventHandler<OrderCompletedEventArgs> handler = (s, e) => DoSomething();
service.OrderCompleted += handler;
// ... later ...
service.OrderCompleted -= handler;    // works — same object

docs.title: Events in ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
Worth knowing: classic C# events are rare in ASP.NET Core applications. They are much more common in desktop UI code (WinForms, WPF).

The reasons are practical. Events are synchronous by default, and there is no clean way to await an event handler. They are in-process only, so they do not survive a restart or cross a service boundary. And the subscription lifetime does not match the request-scoped world that ASP.NET Core lives in.

What is used instead:

  • MediatR notifications for in-process publish/subscribe — see 22.10
  • Domain events raised by entities and dispatched after SaveChanges — see 22.8
  • A message broker (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus) for anything crossing a service boundary — see 23.4

If an interviewer asks about events in a web context, mentioning this distinction is a strong answer.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an event and how does it differ from a delegate?

An event is a delegate with access restrictions applied. With a plain public delegate field, any outside code could assign to it — wiping out all existing subscribers — or invoke it, firing the event from outside the class. The event keyword restricts outside code to += and -= only. Assignment and invocation are limited to the declaring class. So an event is the safe, encapsulated way to expose a delegate as a notification point.

Q: How can events cause a memory leak?

When an object subscribes to an event, the publisher stores a reference to the subscriber's method, which means it holds a reference to the subscriber object. If the publisher is long-lived and the subscriber is short-lived, the subscriber can never be garbage collected even after everything else has released it — because the event is still holding on. The fix is to unsubscribe with -=, usually in Dispose. The trap is that you cannot unsubscribe a lambda unless you stored it in a variable first, because writing the same lambda again creates a completely different object.

Q: Why do you write MyEvent?.Invoke(...) instead of just MyEvent(...)?

Because if nobody has subscribed, the delegate is null and calling it throws. The null-conditional operator handles that. It also avoids a race condition that the older if (MyEvent != null) MyEvent(...) pattern has — another thread could unsubscribe the last handler between the check and the call. ?.Invoke reads the delegate once into a temporary and calls that, so the value it checked is the value it calls.

Q: Do you use C# events in ASP.NET Core?

Rarely. They are synchronous, you cannot properly await a handler, and they only work within a single process, so they do not fit a web application well. For in-process notifications I would use MediatR notifications or domain events dispatched after saving changes. For anything crossing a service boundary I would use a message broker, because that also gives you durability and retries. Events are much more at home in desktop UI frameworks.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting to unsubscribe leaks the subscriber. The publisher keeps it alive.
  • You cannot unsubscribe a lambda by writing it again. Store it in a variable.
  • A throwing handler stops the remaining handlers. They are invoked in order and the exception propagates.
  • Handlers run on whatever thread raised the event. There is no automatic marshalling and no automatic thread safety.
  • async void event handlers swallow exceptions and can crash the process. This is one of the very few places async void is tolerated, and it still needs a try/catch around the whole body. See 2.15.
  • Events cannot be awaited. If handlers need to do async work, an event is the wrong tool.

docs.title: 1.13 — Lambda Expressions and Closures
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.12 Events · Next: 1.14 Extension methods

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A lambda is a short way to write a method inline. x => x * 2 is a whole method.
  • A closure happens when a lambda uses a variable from the code around it. The compiler quietly moves that variable onto the heap so the lambda can still reach it later.
  • Closures capture the variable itself, not its value at that moment. That is the trap, and it bites hardest inside loops.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A lambda is just a method without a name, written where you need it.

// A normal method
static bool IsExpensive(Order o) { return o.Total > 100; }

// The same thing as a lambda
o => o.Total > 100

Read => as "goes to" or "becomes". So o => o.Total > 100 reads as "an order becomes whether its total is over 100".

A closure is what happens when a lambda reaches out and uses a variable from outside itself. The lambda "closes over" that variable — it keeps hold of it.

This sounds harmless. It is where the interesting behaviour, and the classic bug, comes from.

docs.title: Lambda syntax
docs.text:
() => 42                              // no parameters
x => x * 2                            // one parameter, brackets optional
(x, y) => x + y                       // two parameters, brackets required
(int x, int y) => x + y               // explicit types when inference fails

x =>                                  // multiple statements need braces
{
    var doubled = x * 2;
    return doubled + 1;
}

docs.title: What a closure actually does
docs.text:
Here is a lambda that uses a variable from outside:

int threshold = 100;
Func<Order, bool> isExpensive = o => o.Total > threshold;

threshold is a local variable. Normally, when the method it lives in finishes, it disappears. But the lambda might be called much later, so the variable has to survive.

The compiler solves this by secretly rewriting your code. It creates a hidden class, moves threshold into it as a field, and makes both your method and the lambda use that field instead of a local variable.

Roughly, the compiler turns the code above into something like this:

// Compiler-generated, you never see this
class HiddenClosure
{
    public int threshold;
    public bool IsExpensive(Order o) => o.Total > this.threshold;
}

var closure = new HiddenClosure();
closure.threshold = 100;
Func<Order, bool> isExpensive = closure.IsExpensive;

Two consequences follow from this, and both matter:

  1. There is a heap allocation. Every closure creates one of these hidden objects.
  2. The lambda shares the variable — it does not copy it. Both your method and the lambda are now reading and writing the same field.

That second point is the whole trap.

docs.title: The trap: capturing a variable, not a value
docs.text:
var actions = new List<Action>();

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    actions.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(i));
}

foreach (var a in actions) a();

What do you expect? Most people say 0 1 2.

In older C# the answer was 3 3 3.

Why? Because there is only one i variable for the whole loop. All three lambdas captured that same variable. By the time you ran them, the loop had finished and i had reached 3. All three read the same field, and that field said 3.

The fix is to give each iteration its own variable:

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
{
    int copy = i;                          // a NEW variable each iteration
    actions.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(copy));
}
// Now prints 0 1 2

Important modern update: C# 5 changed foreach so that the loop variable is a fresh variable each iteration. So foreach is safe now:

foreach (var item in items)
    actions.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(item));   // safe since C# 5

But a classic for loop still has one variable, so for loops still have this problem. If you remember one thing: foreach is safe, for is not.

docs.title: Avoiding the allocation
docs.text:
If a lambda does not use anything from around it, the compiler does not need a closure at all — it can cache a single instance and reuse it forever.

// No capture — free, cached by the compiler
items.Where(x => x.IsActive);

// Captures 'minimum' — allocates a closure object every time this runs
items.Where(x => x.Total > minimum);

In a hot loop you can avoid the allocation by passing the value through instead, when the API supports it:

// Some APIs take a 'state' parameter exactly for this reason
cache.GetOrCreate(key, state: minimum, static (entry, min) => Compute(min));

The static keyword on a lambda (C# 9+) tells the compiler "this lambda must not capture anything". If you accidentally capture something, you get a compile error instead of a silent allocation. It is a good habit in performance-sensitive code:

items.Where(static x => x.IsActive);   // compiler-enforced: no captures

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic version of the loop bug, which does show up in real code:

// BUG: all tasks use the same 'i'
var tasks = new List<Task>();
for (int i = 0; i < files.Count; i++)
{
    tasks.Add(Task.Run(() => ProcessFile(files[i])));
    // By the time these run, i == files.Count
    // → IndexOutOfRangeException, or every task processes the same file
}
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

// FIXED: each iteration captures its own copy
var tasks = new List<Task>();
for (int i = 0; i < files.Count; i++)
{
    var index = i;                    // fresh variable per iteration
    tasks.Add(Task.Run(() => ProcessFile(files[index])));
}
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

// BETTER: foreach avoids the whole problem, and reads more clearly
var tasks = files.Select(file => Task.Run(() => ProcessFile(file)));
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

This bug is especially nasty because it is timing-dependent. If the tasks happen to run fast enough, you might get correct results in testing and wrong results in production.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is a closure?

It is what happens when a lambda or anonymous method uses a variable from the scope around it. The compiler cannot let that variable disappear when the method returns, because the lambda might run later. So it generates a hidden class, moves the variable into it as a field, and rewrites both the outer method and the lambda to use that field. The result is that the lambda and the surrounding code share one variable rather than each having a copy.

Q: What is the classic closure bug in a loop?

If you create lambdas inside a for loop and capture the loop variable, every lambda captures the same variable, not its value at that moment. So when you run them afterwards, they all see the final value. A loop from 0 to 2 gives you three lambdas that all print 3. The fix is to copy the loop variable into a new variable inside the loop body, so each iteration gets its own. Worth adding that C# 5 changed foreach so its variable is fresh each iteration — so foreach is safe, but a plain for loop still has the problem.

Q: Do closures have a performance cost?

Yes. Every time a lambda captures something, a hidden object gets allocated on the heap to hold the captured variables, plus a delegate object. In normal code that is irrelevant, but in a hot path called thousands of times per second it adds real garbage collection pressure. A lambda that captures nothing is free, because the compiler caches a single instance. You can mark a lambda static to make the compiler prove it captures nothing.

Q: What does static on a lambda do?

It tells the compiler the lambda is not allowed to capture any variable from the surrounding scope. If you try, you get a compile error. It is useful in performance-critical code because it turns an accidental allocation into something the compiler catches for you, and it documents the intent clearly.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Capturing a for loop variable. All lambdas share one variable. foreach is safe since C# 5; for is not.
  • The captured variable is shared both ways. If the outer code changes it after the lambda is created, the lambda sees the new value.
  • A closure keeps the whole captured object alive. If a lambda captures this implicitly by using a field, it keeps the entire containing object from being collected. That is a common leak in event handlers — see 1.12.
  • Closures allocate. Two objects, in fact — the closure and the delegate. Fine normally, expensive in a tight loop.
  • Capturing a ref, out, or in parameter is not allowed. Nor is capturing a Span<T>, because those cannot live on the heap.
  • Async lambdas that capture large objects hold them for the whole operation, not just until the first await.

docs.title: 1.14 — Extension Methods
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.13 Lambdas and closures · Next: 1.15 Nullability

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An extension method lets you add a method to a type you do not own — string, int, a NuGet library's class — without changing or inheriting from it.
  • The recipe: a static method, in a static class, with this on the first parameter.
  • It is only syntax. The compiler turns text.Slugify() into StringExtensions.Slugify(text). Nothing is really added to the type.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a method on a type you cannot edit. You cannot add Slugify() to string — it is sealed and it belongs to Microsoft.

Your options without extension methods are all a bit ugly:

StringHelper.Slugify(title);          // works, but reads backwards

An extension method lets you write it the natural way:

title.Slugify();                      // reads like it belongs there

Nothing magic happens. The type is not modified. The compiler simply sees title.Slugify(), finds no such method on string, then goes looking for an extension method that fits — and rewrites your call into StringExtensions.Slugify(title).

That is why the first big limitation exists: an extension method can only use the public members of the type. It is outside code, so it has no special access.

LINQ is the most famous example. Where, Select and OrderBy are all extension methods on IEnumerable<T>. That is how Microsoft added them to every collection ever written, including ones that existed before LINQ, without changing a single one of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Three requirements, all mandatory:

  1. The class must be static
  2. The method must be static
  3. The first parameter must have this in front of it
public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static string Slugify(this string value)
    {
        return string.Join('-', value.ToLowerInvariant().Split(' '));
    }
}

Now:

"Hello World Again".Slugify();   // "hello-world-again"

// Which the compiler turns into:
StringExtensions.Slugify("Hello World Again");

Extra parameters come after the this one:

public static string Truncate(this string value, int maxLength)
    => value.Length <= maxLength ? value : value[..maxLength] + "…";

description.Truncate(100);

docs.title: You must import the namespace
docs.text:
The compiler only finds extension methods whose namespace is in scope. If your extension lives in MyApp.Extensions, any file using it needs using MyApp.Extensions;.

This is the number one cause of "why is my extension method not showing up in IntelliSense". A useful trick is to put widely used extensions in a namespace you already import everywhere, or add a global using so it is available in every file (see 1.26).

docs.title: Real methods always win
docs.text:
If the type has an actual method with the same name and a matching signature, the real method is used and your extension is silently ignored.

public static class MyExtensions
{
    public static string ToString(this object obj) => "mine";
}

someObject.ToString();   // calls the REAL ToString. Yours never runs.

No warning, no error — it just quietly does not work. There is a good reason for this rule: it means a library adding a new method in a future version cannot be hijacked by someone else's extension. But it does make for a confusing debugging session.

docs.title: Extensions work on null
docs.text:
This surprises people. Because it is really a static method call, this can be null without throwing:

public static bool IsBlank(this string? value)
    => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value);

string? name = null;
name.IsBlank();   // true — no NullReferenceException!

If this were a real instance method, calling it on null would throw immediately. Since it is a static call with null passed as an argument, it works fine.

This is occasionally useful, but be careful — it violates the reader's expectation that calling a method on null blows up.

docs.title: Extensions on interfaces
docs.text:
This is the most powerful use, and it is exactly how LINQ works:

public static class EnumerableExtensions
{
    public static IEnumerable<IReadOnlyList<T>> Chunk<T>(
        this IEnumerable<T> source, int size)
    {
        var batch = new List<T>(size);
        foreach (var item in source)
        {
            batch.Add(item);
            if (batch.Count == size)
            {
                yield return batch;
                batch = new List<T>(size);
            }
        }
        if (batch.Count > 0) yield return batch;
    }
}

Write it once against IEnumerable<T>, and it works on every collection type in .NET — arrays, lists, sets, database queries, everything.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The most common real use in ASP.NET Core is tidying up service registration:

public static class ServiceCollectionExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrderModule(
        this IServiceCollection services,
        IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
        services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
        services.Configure<OrderOptions>(config.GetSection("Orders"));
        return services;                       // return it so calls can chain
    }
}

Which turns a long Program.cs into this:

builder.Services
    .AddOrderModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddPaymentModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddNotificationModule(builder.Configuration);

Notice the method returns IServiceCollection. That is what allows the chaining. Every Add... method in ASP.NET Core follows this pattern, and it is worth copying — it keeps Program.cs readable as an application grows, and it keeps each module's registrations next to that module's code.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an extension method and how do you write one?

It is a way to add a method to an existing type without modifying it or inheriting from it. You write a static method inside a static class, and put the this keyword on the first parameter — that parameter is the type you are extending. The compiler then lets you call it as though it were an instance method. Behind the scenes nothing is added to the type; the compiler just rewrites value.MyMethod() into MyClass.MyMethod(value).

Q: What are the limitations?

Three main ones. It can only use the public members of the type, because it really is outside code — no access to private fields. If the type has a real method with the same signature, that real method always wins and your extension is silently ignored. And the namespace has to be imported, otherwise the compiler will not find it at all, which is the usual reason someone's extension method does not appear.

Q: Can you call an extension method on a null reference?

Yes, and that surprises people. Because it compiles down to a static method call with the value passed as an ordinary argument, null is a perfectly valid argument. So an extension like IsBlank() can handle a null string without throwing. It is occasionally handy, but worth using carefully, because most readers assume that calling a method on null will throw.

Q: Where do you use them in ASP.NET Core?

Most commonly for grouping service registrations. Rather than 40 lines of services.AddScoped<...> in Program.cs, each module exposes an AddSomethingModule(this IServiceCollection services) extension that returns the collection so calls can chain. LINQ itself is entirely extension methods on IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T>, and ASP.NET Core's whole configuration API — UseRouting, UseAuthentication, MapControllers — is built the same way.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting the using. The method exists but the compiler cannot see it. This is the most common problem by far.
  • A real method silently wins. No warning that your extension was ignored.
  • They cannot access private members. If you need that, you need a real method.
  • They cannot be used to implement an interface. A type does not satisfy IFoo just because an extension method supplies the missing member.
  • Do not extend object. It puts your method on absolutely everything, cluttering IntelliSense across the entire codebase.
  • Overusing them hides where the code lives. If a method genuinely belongs on the type and you own the type, put it on the type.
  • Extension methods cannot be virtual or overridden. Resolution happens at compile time based on the declared type, so they do not take part in polymorphism.
