docs.title: 1.15 — Nullable Value Types and Nullable Reference Types
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.14 Extension methods · Next: 1.16 Null operators

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Nullable value types (int?) are real. They are a struct that wraps a value plus a "has it got one?" flag.
  • Nullable reference types (string?) are not real. They are compiler warnings only. Nothing changes at runtime.
  • That difference is the whole interview question. string? and string compile to exactly the same thing.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These two features look similar and work completely differently. Understanding why is the point of this topic.

Nullable value types solve a genuine problem. An int cannot be null — it always holds a number. But sometimes you need "no value": a database column that allows NULL, an optional form field. So .NET provides int?, which is really Nullable<int> — a small struct holding an int plus a bool saying whether it is set.

Nullable reference types solve a different problem. A string could always be null, and the compiler never warned you. So C# 8 added a way to say "this one should never be null, warn me if I might be breaking that."

The critical difference:

Nullable value types Nullable reference types Since C# 2 (2005) C# 8 (2019) Real at runtime? Yes — a different type No — compiler warnings only Enforced? Yes, by the type system No, nothing at runtime

docs.title: Nullable value types — real
docs.text:
int? age = null;         // really Nullable<int>
int? score = 42;

age.HasValue;            // false
score.HasValue;          // true
score.Value;             // 42 — throws InvalidOperationException if null

int definite = score ?? 0;                 // 42
int fromNull = age ?? 0;                   // 0

if (score is int actualScore)              // pattern matching unwraps it
    Console.WriteLine(actualScore * 2);

Because it is a real type, the compiler genuinely stops you doing unsafe things:

int? maybe = null;
int definite = maybe;      // COMPILE ERROR — no automatic conversion
int definite = maybe.Value;  // compiles, but THROWS at runtime if null

docs.title: Nullable reference types — just warnings
docs.text:
Turn it on in your .csproj (this is the default in new .NET projects):

<Nullable>enable</Nullable>

Now the meaning of your declarations changes:

string name = "Ada";       // "I promise this is never null"
string? nickname = null;   // "this might be null"

The compiler now tracks this and warns you:

string name = null;
// WARNING CS8600: Converting null literal to non-nullable type

string? nickname = GetNickname();
Console.WriteLine(nickname.Length);
// WARNING CS8602: Dereference of a possibly null reference

But watch this:

string? a = null;
string  b = null!;      // the ! silences the warning

// Both of these are just "null" at runtime. Identical.
// The generated code is byte-for-byte the same.

There is no runtime check. If null arrives from somewhere the compiler could not see — JSON deserialization, a database, reflection, or older code compiled without the feature — it flows straight through and you get a NullReferenceException exactly as before.

So the honest summary is: nullable reference types are a very good linting tool, not a guarantee. Saying that in an interview shows you actually understand the feature rather than having read the headline.

docs.title: The null-forgiving operator !
docs.text:
! tells the compiler "trust me, this is not null":

var user = _users.FirstOrDefault(u => u.Id == id)!;   // I know it exists

It suppresses the warning and does absolutely nothing else. No check, no exception. If you are wrong, you get a NullReferenceException later at a more confusing place.

Treat every ! as a small piece of technical debt. Sometimes it is genuinely correct — when you know something the compiler cannot — but if a file is full of them, the annotations are wrong somewhere.

docs.title: Where null still gets in
docs.text:
The compiler analyses your code. It cannot analyse the outside world.

public class Person
{
    public string Name { get; set; }    // declared non-nullable
}

var p = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person>("{}");
Console.WriteLine(p.Name.Length);
// Name is NULL at runtime. No warning was given.
// The deserializer set fields directly and ignored your annotation.

The same applies to Entity Framework materialising entities, reflection, and any library compiled before nullable reference types existed.

The practical rule: annotations are documentation and a safety net inside your own code. At the boundaries — HTTP input, database rows, external APIs — you still need real validation. See 11.4.

docs.title: Making it useful
docs.text:
For properties, combine with required so the compiler actually enforces initialisation:

public class Person
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }   // must be set — compile error if not
    public string? Nickname { get; init; }       // genuinely optional
}

Without required, a non-nullable property produces a warning at the declaration and then everyone ignores it. With required, forgetting it is a hard error at the call site.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic method showing the annotations doing real work:

public async Task<OrderDto?> GetOrderAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order = await _db.Orders
        .Include(o => o.Customer)
        .FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);

    // The '?' on the return type tells callers: this can be null.
    // The compiler will warn them if they forget to check.
    if (order is null) return null;

    return new OrderDto
    {
        Id = order.Id,
        // Customer is a navigation property — could be null if Include failed
        CustomerName = order.Customer?.Name ?? "(unknown)",
        Total = order.Total
    };
}

And the caller — the compiler now forces the check:

var dto = await GetOrderAsync(id, ct);

Console.WriteLine(dto.Total);
// WARNING — dto might be null, you did not check

if (dto is not null)
    Console.WriteLine(dto.Total);   // no warning — the compiler followed your check

That last part is the real value. The compiler tracks the flow of your code. Once you check for null, it knows the variable is safe for the rest of that branch.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between a nullable value type and a nullable reference type?

A nullable value type like int? is real — it is Nullable<int>, a struct that holds the value plus a flag saying whether it is set. The type system genuinely enforces it, so you cannot assign an int? to an int without handling the null case. A nullable reference type like string? is not real at all. It is purely a compile-time annotation that turns on warnings. At runtime string? and string are the exact same type and produce identical code. So one is a type-system feature, and the other is a static analysis feature wearing similar syntax.

Q: Do nullable reference types prevent null reference exceptions?

No, and this is the most important thing to understand about them. They help you find places where null might flow, and if you fix every warning your own code becomes much safer. But nothing is checked at runtime. Null can still arrive from JSON deserialization, from Entity Framework, from reflection, or from a library compiled without the feature — and none of those respect your annotations. So they are an excellent linting tool, not a guarantee. You still need real validation at your application's boundaries.

Q: What does the ! operator do?

It is the null-forgiving operator. It tells the compiler "I know this looks like it could be null, but trust me, it is not" and suppresses the warning. It generates no code and performs no check. It is sometimes legitimately needed when you know something the compiler's flow analysis cannot work out, but each use is a small piece of debt. A file full of them usually means the annotations are wrong somewhere rather than that the compiler is being unhelpful.

Q: How do you handle nullability on an API model?

I mark genuinely optional properties as nullable and mandatory ones as non-nullable and required, so forgetting one is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. But I do not rely on that for incoming HTTP data, because model binding and deserialization can bypass it. For real input I use validation attributes or FluentValidation, so a missing field produces a proper 400 response with a clear message rather than a null reference exception deep in the handler.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Nullable reference types are compile-time only. They enforce nothing at runtime.
  • Deserialization ignores them completely. JsonSerializer will happily leave a non-nullable property null and never warn you.
  • ! hides the problem rather than fixing it. It moves the crash somewhere less obvious.
  • A non-nullable property without required or an initialiser gives a warning where it is declared, which people learn to ignore, rather than an error where it matters.
  • int? cannot be assigned to int without handling null. .Value throws InvalidOperationException — note, not NullReferenceException — if there is no value.
  • Nullable<T> cannot be nested. There is no int??.
  • Turning <Nullable>enable</Nullable> on in an existing project produces hundreds of warnings. Enable it per-file with #nullable enable and work through gradually.

docs.title: 1.16 — Null-Handling Operators
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.15 Nullability · Next: 1.17 Pattern matching

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• ?? — "use this instead if the left side is null".
  • ?. — "only carry on if this is not null, otherwise give me null".
  • ??= — "assign this only if the variable is currently null".
  • A chain of ?. stops at the first null and returns null for the whole expression.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These four operators exist to replace long, noisy null checks with short ones. That is their whole purpose — they add no new capability, just less typing and less clutter.

Before them, guarding against null looked like this:

string city;
if (order != null && order.Customer != null && order.Customer.Address != null)
    city = order.Customer.Address.City;
else
    city = "Unknown";

After:

string city = order?.Customer?.Address?.City ?? "Unknown";

Same behaviour, one line, and much easier to read once the symbols are familiar.

docs.title: ?? — null-coalescing
docs.text:
"If the left side is null, use the right side instead."

string? name = null;
string display = name ?? "Anonymous";      // "Anonymous"

string? found = "Ada";
string display2 = found ?? "Anonymous";    // "Ada"

It only triggers on null, not on empty or zero:

string empty = "";
string result = empty ?? "fallback";       // "" — empty string is NOT null
int zero = 0;
int? maybe = 0;
int r = maybe ?? 99;                       // 0 — zero is a real value

You can chain it. It uses the first non-null it finds:

var value = fromCache ?? fromDatabase ?? fromDefault ?? "last resort";

It is also short-circuiting — if the left side is not null, the right side is never evaluated:

var config = cached ?? LoadFromDisk();
// LoadFromDisk() only runs if 'cached' is null. No wasted work.

docs.title: ?. — null-conditional
docs.text:
"If this is null, stop and give back null. Otherwise carry on."

string? name = null;
int? length = name?.Length;      // null — Length was never called

string? real = "Ada";
int? length2 = real?.Length;     // 3

Two things to notice:

The result becomes nullable. name.Length would be an int, but name?.Length is an int?, because it now has a way to produce "no answer".

A chain stops at the first null. It does not keep going and crash:

order?.Customer?.Address?.City
// If 'order' is null → the whole thing is null.
// Customer, Address and City are never touched.

There is also an indexer version:

var first = list?[0];            // null if list is null

And it works for method calls, which is how you safely raise events:

OrderCompleted?.Invoke(this, args);   // does nothing if nobody subscribed

See 1.12 for why this specific use also avoids a race condition.

docs.title: ??= — null-coalescing assignment
docs.text:
"Assign this only if the variable is currently null."

string? name = null;
name ??= "Default";        // name is now "Default"
name ??= "Something else"; // no effect — name is not null any more

Which is shorthand for:

if (name is null)
    name = "Default";

It is very handy for lazy initialisation:

private List<string>? _items;
public List<string> Items => _items ??= LoadItems();
// LoadItems() runs on the first access only.
// Note: this is NOT thread-safe. Use Lazy<T> if several threads may hit it.

docs.title: The one that catches people out
docs.text:
int? count = list?.Count ?? 0;

Read the precedence carefully: ?. binds tighter than ??. So this is (list?.Count) ?? 0 — if list is null the whole list?.Count is null, and then ?? supplies 0. That is what you want.

But this is different:

var length = person?.Name.Length;
// If person is null → null, fine.
// If person is NOT null but Name IS null → NullReferenceException!
// The ?. only guarded 'person', not 'Name'.

Every link in the chain needs its own ?.:

var length = person?.Name?.Length;   // now both are guarded

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Realistic before-and-after:

// BEFORE — correct, but hard to read
public string GetShippingCity(Order order)
{
    if (order == null) return "Unknown";
    if (order.Customer == null) return "Unknown";
    if (order.Customer.ShippingAddress == null) return "Unknown";
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(order.Customer.ShippingAddress.City)) return "Unknown";
    return order.Customer.ShippingAddress.City;
}

// AFTER — same behaviour
public string GetShippingCity(Order? order)
{
    var city = order?.Customer?.ShippingAddress?.City;
    return string.IsNullOrEmpty(city) ? "Unknown" : city;
}

Note that ?? alone would not be enough here, because an empty string is not null. The requirement was "unknown if missing or blank", so it still needs an explicit check. This is a very common mistake — reaching for ?? when you actually need string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between ?? and ?.?

?? supplies a fallback value when the left side is null — name ?? "Anonymous" gives you the name, or "Anonymous" if it is null. ?. stops a member access when the thing on the left is null and returns null for the whole expression instead of throwing. So ?? is about supplying a default, and ?. is about safely skipping. They are usually used together: order?.Customer?.Name ?? "Unknown".

Q: Does ?? treat an empty string as null?

No. It only checks for null. An empty string, a zero, and false are all real values and pass straight through. That trips people up when they use ?? for what is really a "is this missing or blank" check — for strings you usually want string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace instead.

Q: What happens in a long ?. chain if something in the middle is null?

The whole expression short-circuits and evaluates to null. Nothing after the null link is evaluated at all. But every link needs its own ?. — writing a?.B.C only protects against a being null, so if B turns out to be null you still get a NullReferenceException. You need a?.B?.C.

Q: Where is ??= useful?

Lazy initialisation, mainly — _cache ??= BuildCache() runs the expensive work only on first access. It is worth remembering that it is not thread-safe, so if several threads could hit it at once you want Lazy<T> instead.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• ?? only checks null. Empty string, 0 and false all pass through as valid values.
  • Every link in a chain needs its own ?.. a?.B.C does not protect B.
  • ?. makes the result nullable. int becomes int?, which can cause a surprising compile error further along.
  • ??= is not thread-safe. Two threads can both see null and both assign. Use Lazy<T> for that.
  • ?. can hide real bugs. If something should never be null, silently returning null turns a loud crash into a quiet wrong answer that shows up much later.
  • ?. does not work with await directly. await task?.RunAsync() fails, because you cannot await a null Task. You need an explicit check.

docs.text:

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Pattern matching lets you test a value's shape and pull data out of it in one step.
  • A switch expression (=> arms) returns a value. A switch statement (case: labels) runs code. Prefer the expression.
  • is null and is not null are safer than == null, because == can be overloaded and pattern matching cannot.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Pattern matching answers "does this value look like X?" and, if so, gives you the pieces.

The old way needed three separate steps — check the type, cast it, then use it:

if (shape is Circle)
{
    var circle = (Circle)shape;      // check again, then cast
    return Math.PI * circle.Radius * circle.Radius;
}

Pattern matching does all three at once:

if (shape is Circle circle)
    return Math.PI * circle.Radius * circle.Radius;

One line. No cast. No chance of the check and the cast getting out of sync.

docs.title: Type pattern
docs.text:
if (value is string text)
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);      // 'text' is already a string here

The variable is only in scope where the check succeeded, so the compiler guarantees it is valid.

docs.title: Constant and null patterns
docs.text:
if (status is 404) { }
if (name is null) { }
if (name is not null) { }

Prefer is null over == null. Here is why: == can be overloaded by a type, so x == null might run somebody's custom code that does something unexpected. is null cannot be overloaded — it always means exactly "is this reference null". In a class with a custom ==, they can genuinely disagree.

docs.title: Relational and logical patterns (C# 9)
docs.text:
You can compare, and combine with and, or, not:

if (age is >= 18 and < 65) { }
if (statusCode is 401 or 403) { }
if (input is not null and not "") { }

Read age is >= 18 and < 65 as "age is at least 18 and under 65". Note you do not repeat the variable name — that is the point of the syntax.

docs.title: Property pattern
docs.text:
Match on the values inside an object:

if (order is { Status: OrderStatus.Pending, Total: > 1000 })
{
    // order is not null, AND its Status is Pending, AND its Total is over 1000
}

That single line replaces a null check plus two property comparisons. Note it also handles null for you — { ... } never matches null.

You can nest and extract:

if (order is { Customer.Address.Country: "UK", Total: var total })
{
    Console.WriteLine($"UK order worth {total}");
}

var total captures the value into a new variable while matching.

docs.title: Switch expressions
docs.text:
A switch expression produces a value. Notice => instead of case: and break:

// Old switch statement
string GetLabel(OrderStatus status)
{
    switch (status)
    {
        case OrderStatus.Pending:   return "Waiting";
        case OrderStatus.Shipped:   return "On its way";
        case OrderStatus.Delivered: return "Complete";
        default:                    throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException();
    }
}

// Switch expression — same thing
string GetLabel(OrderStatus status) => status switch
{
    OrderStatus.Pending   => "Waiting",
    OrderStatus.Shipped   => "On its way",
    OrderStatus.Delivered => "Complete",
    _                     => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(status))
};

The _ at the bottom is the discard pattern — it matches anything, so it plays the role of default.

A big advantage: the compiler checks you covered everything. If you add a new value to OrderStatus and forget to handle it, you get a warning that the switch is not exhaustive. A switch statement gives you nothing.

Switch expressions can use any pattern, and you can add a when clause for conditions that do not fit a pattern:

decimal CalculateDiscount(Customer c) => c switch
{
    { IsVip: true, YearsActive: > 5 } => 0.20m,
    { IsVip: true }                   => 0.10m,
    { OrderCount: > 100 }             => 0.05m,
    _ when DateTime.Today.DayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.Friday => 0.02m,
    _                                 => 0m
};

Order matters. Arms are checked top to bottom and the first match wins. If you put { IsVip: true } above { IsVip: true, YearsActive: > 5 }, the more specific one can never be reached — and the compiler will warn you about that too.

docs.title: List patterns (C# 11)
docs.text:
int[] numbers = [1, 2, 3];

if (numbers is [1, 2, 3]) { }              // exactly these three
if (numbers is [1, ..]) { }                // starts with 1
if (numbers is [_, _, var last]) { }       // three items, capture the last
if (numbers is [var first, .., var final]) { }   // at least two, capture the ends

.. is the "slice" pattern, meaning "any number of items here".

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic example — mapping exceptions to HTTP responses:

public static ProblemDetails ToProblemDetails(this Exception ex) => ex switch
{
    NotFoundException nf => new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = 404,
        Title  = "Not found",
        Detail = nf.Message
    },

    ValidationException { Errors.Count: > 0 } ve => new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = 400,
        Title  = "Validation failed",
        Detail = string.Join("; ", ve.Errors)
    },

    UnauthorizedAccessException => new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = 403,
        Title  = "Forbidden"
    },

    OperationCanceledException => new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = 499,
        Title  = "Request cancelled"
    },

    _ => new ProblemDetails
    {
        Status = 500,
        Title  = "An unexpected error occurred"
        // deliberately no Detail — never leak internals to the client
    }
};

Read it top to bottom and it is obvious what maps to what. The equivalent if / else if chain with casts would be roughly three times as long and much easier to get wrong.

This is a very common shape in real ASP.NET Core code — see 5.12.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is pattern matching?

It is testing whether a value has a particular shape and extracting parts of it in the same step. The simplest form is the type pattern — if (x is Circle c) checks the type and gives you a strongly-typed variable at once, replacing the old check-then-cast pair. It extends to constants, ranges, properties, tuples and lists, and it combines with and, or and not. The practical benefit is that it removes a whole class of bug where the check and the cast drift apart.

Q: What is the difference between a switch statement and a switch expression?

A switch statement is a control-flow construct — it runs code, uses case: labels, and each branch needs break or return. A switch expression produces a value, uses => arms separated by commas, and can be assigned or returned directly. The expression form is usually better: it is shorter, it cannot fall through by accident, and the compiler warns you if you have not covered every case, which means adding a new enum value gets flagged rather than silently falling through to the default.

Q: Why prefer is null over == null?

Because == can be overloaded by the type, so x == null could invoke custom code that does something unexpected — or that throws. is null cannot be overloaded; it always means "is this reference actually null". So it is both more predictable and slightly faster. The same goes for is not null over != null.

Q: What does the when clause do in a switch?

It adds a condition that cannot be expressed as a pattern. Patterns can test types, values, ranges and properties, but they cannot call methods or reference other variables. when lets you attach an arbitrary boolean condition to an arm, so you might write _ when DateTime.Today.DayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.Friday => 0.02m.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Arm order matters. The first match wins, so a general pattern above a specific one makes the specific one unreachable. The compiler warns about this — do not ignore it.
  • A switch expression with no match throws at runtime. If nothing matches and there is no _ arm, you get a SwitchExpressionException. Either cover everything or add _.
  • { } never matches null. So x is { } is actually a null check in disguise, which is clever but confusing to read. Prefer x is not null.
  • == and is can disagree on a type with a custom == operator.
  • Deeply nested property patterns become unreadable fast. Two levels is usually the limit before a named method is clearer.
  • var in a pattern always matches, including null. x is var y is always true, which makes it useless as a test — it is only for capturing.

docs.title: 1.18 — Tuples, Deconstruction, ref / out / in
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.17 Pattern matching · Next: 1.19 Indexers and operators

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A tuple lets a method return several values without declaring a class: (bool ok, string error).
  • out = the method must assign it. ref = it must already have a value, and the method can change it. in = pass by reference but read-only.
  • Tuples are great inside your code. Do not use them on a public API — named types document themselves.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A method can only return one thing. But sometimes you genuinely have two answers: "did it work, and if so what is the result?"

There are four ways to handle that, and knowing when each fits is the point of this topic:

  1. Return a tuple — quick, no ceremony
  2. Use an out parameter — the classic TryParse style
  3. Return a small record — clearest for anything public
  4. Return a Result type — best when failure carries information

docs.title: Tuples
docs.text:
// Returning two values with no class needed
public (bool Success, string? Error) Validate(Order order)
{
    if (order.Total <= 0)
        return (false, "Total must be positive");

    return (true, null);
}

Using it:

var result = Validate(order);
if (!result.Success)
    Console.WriteLine(result.Error);

Notice you get real names — Success and Error, not Item1 and Item2. Naming the elements in the return type is what makes tuples readable. Without names you get:

public (bool, string?) Validate(Order o) { ... }

var r = Validate(order);
if (!r.Item1) Console.WriteLine(r.Item2);    // what are these? Unreadable.

Always name your tuple elements.

docs.title: Deconstruction
docs.text:
You can split a tuple straight into separate variables:

var (success, error) = Validate(order);
if (!success) Console.WriteLine(error);

Or discard the parts you do not need with _:

var (_, error) = Validate(order);

Records get deconstruction for free (1.2), and you can add it to any class by writing a Deconstruct method:

public class Point(int x, int y)
{
    public void Deconstruct(out int x2, out int y2) { x2 = x; y2 = y; }
}

var (x, y) = new Point(3, 4);

Deconstruction also works nicely with dictionaries:

foreach (var (key, value) in dictionary)
    Console.WriteLine($"{key} = {value}");

docs.title: out — the method must fill it in
docs.text:
if (int.TryParse(input, out int number))
    Console.WriteLine(number * 2);
else
    Console.WriteLine("Not a number");

Rules for out:

  • The caller does not need to initialise it beforehand.
  • The method must assign it before returning, on every path. The compiler enforces this.
  • You can declare the variable inline, as above, which is the modern style.

The Try... pattern is the standard use: return a bool for success, put the actual value in an out parameter. It is used everywhere in .NET — int.TryParse, dictionary.TryGetValue, DateTime.TryParseExact.

You can discard an out you do not care about:

if (int.TryParse(input, out _))
    Console.WriteLine("It is a number, I just do not need the value");

docs.title: ref — pass the variable itself
docs.text:
static void Double(ref int value) => value *= 2;

int x = 5;
Double(ref x);      // x is now 10

Rules for ref:

  • The variable must already have a value before the call.
  • The method may read it and change it.
  • You must write ref at both the declaration and the call site.

That last rule is deliberate. Because ref means "this method might change my variable", C# forces you to write it at the call site so the reader can see it happening.

ref is rarely needed in everyday code. Its main modern uses are performance work with large structs, and interop with non-.NET code.

docs.title: in — pass by reference, but read-only
docs.text:
static double Distance(in Point a, in Point b)
{
    // a and b cannot be modified here — the compiler enforces it
    return Math.Sqrt(Math.Pow(a.X - b.X, 2) + Math.Pow(a.Y - b.Y, 2));
}

in exists purely for performance with large structs. Normally passing a struct copies the whole thing. in passes a reference instead, avoiding the copy, while still promising the method will not modify it.

For a small struct it is not worth it — the reference is about the same size as the value. It only pays off once the struct is bigger than roughly 16–24 bytes. And it works best with readonly struct, because otherwise the compiler sometimes has to make a defensive copy anyway, which defeats the purpose.

docs.title: Quick comparison
docs.text: Must be initialised before? Can the method change it? Write keyword at call site? out No Must assign it Yes ref Yes Yes Yes in Yes No Optional

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Choosing between the approaches — this is what an interviewer is really testing:

// TUPLE — fine for a private helper, quick and readable
private (decimal Subtotal, decimal Tax) CalculateTotals(Order order)
{
    var subtotal = order.Lines.Sum(l => l.Price * l.Quantity);
    return (subtotal, subtotal * 0.2m);
}

// OUT — right when the caller often does not want the value at all
public bool TryGetDiscount(string code, out decimal discount)
{
    discount = 0;
    if (!_codes.TryGetValue(code, out var found)) return false;
    discount = found;
    return true;
}

// RECORD — right for anything public. It documents itself
// and you can add a field later without breaking callers.
public record OrderTotals(decimal Subtotal, decimal Tax, decimal Total);
public OrderTotals CalculateTotals(Order order) { ... }

// RESULT TYPE — right when failure carries real information
public Result<Order> PlaceOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) { ... }

The rule of thumb: tuples inside a class, named types across a public boundary. A tuple in a public API forces every caller to remember what the elements mean, and adding a third element is a breaking change.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: When would you use a tuple instead of a class?

For a private or internal method that genuinely needs to return two or three related values, where creating a whole type would be more ceremony than it is worth. They are quick, they are allocated on the stack since ValueTuple is a struct, and with named elements they read well. But I would not put one on a public API — a named record documents itself, shows up properly in IntelliSense and Swagger, and can gain a property later without breaking callers.

Q: What is the difference between ref and out?

With out, the caller does not have to initialise the variable, but the method is required to assign it before returning — the compiler checks every path. With ref, the variable must already have a value, and the method may read it as well as change it. So out is for "the method gives me a value", and ref is for "the method modifies my existing value". Both require the keyword at the call site so the reader can see that a variable may be changed.

Q: What is in for?

Passing a value type by reference without allowing modification. It exists for performance — a large struct normally gets copied on every call, and in avoids that copy while still guaranteeing the method will not change it. It is only worth using for structs bigger than around 16 to 24 bytes, and it works best with a readonly struct, because otherwise the compiler may make a defensive copy anyway and you gain nothing.

Q: Are tuples value types or reference types?

The modern ones are value types. ValueTuple, which is what the (int, string) syntax creates, is a struct, so it is generally allocated without hitting the heap. The older System.Tuple class is a reference type and is mostly obsolete now. Worth knowing that ValueTuple is mutable and compares by value.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Unnamed tuple elements give you Item1 and Item2. Unreadable. Always name them.
  • Tuple element names are not part of the runtime type. They are compiler metadata, so reflection and some serializers see only Item1/Item2.
  • Tuples in public APIs age badly. Adding an element is a breaking change, and they serialize poorly.
  • ValueTuple is mutable. Unlike a record, you can change its fields, which is occasionally surprising.
  • out parameters cannot be used in async methods. This is a common annoyance — use a tuple or a small result type instead.
  • in can be slower for small structs, because passing a reference and then reading through it costs more than just copying a few bytes.
  • A ref or out parameter cannot be captured by a lambda. See 1.13.

docs.title: 1.19 — Indexers, Operator Overloading, Conversions
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.18 Tuples, ref, out, in · Next: 1.20 Exceptions

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• An indexer lets your class be used with square brackets: myThing["key"].
  • Operator overloading lets you define what +, == and so on mean for your type.
  • implicit conversions happen automatically; explicit ones need a cast. Use explicit whenever the conversion can lose information or fail.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These three features all do the same kind of thing: they let your own type use syntax that normally only works for built-in types.

Used well, they make domain code read naturally — price1 + price2 is clearer than price1.Add(price2). Used badly, they hide behaviour and confuse readers. The interview value is mostly in knowing the rules and the risks.

docs.title: Indexers
docs.text:
An indexer is written like a property, but named this and taking parameters:

public class Settings
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, string> _values = new();

    public string this[string key]
    {
        get => _values.TryGetValue(key, out var v) ? v : "";
        set => _values[key] = value;
    }
}

var settings = new Settings();
settings["theme"] = "dark";      // calls the setter
var theme = settings["theme"];   // calls the getter

Indexers can take any type of parameter, and you can have several overloads:

public Order this[int index] => _orders[index];
public Order? this[Guid id] => _orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == id);

docs.title: Operator overloading
docs.text:
You define what an operator means for your type using public static operator:

public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)
{
    public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b)
    {
        if (a.Currency != b.Currency)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Cannot add different currencies");

        return a with { Amount = a.Amount + b.Amount };
    }

    public static Money operator *(Money m, int quantity)
        => m with { Amount = m.Amount * quantity };

    public static bool operator >(Money a, Money b) => a.Amount > b.Amount;
    public static bool operator <(Money a, Money b) => a.Amount < b.Amount;
}

var total = new Money(10, "GBP") + new Money(5, "GBP");   // Money(15, "GBP")
var bulk  = new Money(10, "GBP") * 3;                     // Money(30, "GBP")

Rules to remember:

  • Operators must be public static.
  • Some must be declared in pairs: == with !=, < with >, <= with >=. The compiler enforces this.
  • If you overload ==, you should also override Equals and GetHashCode, otherwise a == b and a.Equals(b) can give different answers — which breaks dictionaries and LINQ in confusing ways.
  • Some operators cannot be overloaded at all: &&, ||, ??, ?:, =.

Using a record avoids most of this work, since it generates correct Equals, GetHashCode and == for you.

docs.title: Implicit and explicit conversions
docs.text:
public readonly record struct Celsius(double Degrees)
{
    // IMPLICIT — happens automatically, no cast needed
    public static implicit operator double(Celsius c) => c.Degrees;

    // EXPLICIT — requires a cast, because it might not be valid
    public static explicit operator Celsius(double d) =>
        d < -273.15
            ? throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(d), "Below absolute zero")
            : new Celsius(d);
}

Celsius temp = new(20);
double asNumber = temp;                // implicit — just works
Celsius back = (Celsius)25.0;          // explicit — cast required
Celsius bad = (Celsius)(-300.0);       // throws — which is why it is explicit

The rule for choosing: use implicit only when the conversion always succeeds and loses nothing. If it can throw, lose precision, or surprise the reader, make it explicit. The cast then acts as a visible warning at the call site.

This mirrors how the built-in types work. int to long is implicit — always safe. long to int is explicit — it can silently lose data, so you have to ask for it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic strongly-typed ID, which is a common pattern in domain-driven code:

public readonly record struct OrderId(Guid Value)
{
    // Implicit OUT is safe — an OrderId always has a valid Guid
    public static implicit operator Guid(OrderId id) => id.Value;

    // Explicit IN — not every Guid is meant to be an OrderId,
    // so make the conversion visible in the code
    public static explicit operator OrderId(Guid value) => new(value);

    public override string ToString() => Value.ToString();
}

Why bother? Because it stops a whole class of bug:

public void Transfer(OrderId order, CustomerId customer) { }

Transfer(customerId, orderId);
// COMPILE ERROR — the arguments are the wrong way round.
//
// If both were plain Guid, this would compile fine
// and fail mysteriously at runtime.

Two Guid parameters next to each other are very easy to swap by accident. Wrapping them in distinct types makes the compiler catch it. See 22.8.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an indexer?

It lets an instance of your class be accessed with square brackets, like an array or a dictionary. You declare it like a property but name it this and give it parameters. It is useful when your type genuinely represents a collection or a lookup — a settings class, a matrix, a custom collection. It is not something to add just because you can; if the type is not conceptually indexable, a normal named method is clearer.

Q: When should you overload operators?

Only when the operator has an obvious, universally understood meaning for your type. Adding two Money values or two vectors is natural, and a + b reads better than a.Add(b). But if a reader has to stop and work out what your + does, you have made the code worse rather than better. The other important rule is consistency: if you overload ==, you must also override Equals and GetHashCode, otherwise the two ways of comparing can disagree and things like dictionary lookups start behaving strangely.

Q: What is the difference between an implicit and an explicit conversion operator?

An implicit conversion happens automatically with no cast, so it should only be used when the conversion always succeeds and never loses information. An explicit conversion requires a cast at the call site, which acts as a visible signal that something could go wrong. The built-in types follow the same rule — int to long is implicit because it is always safe, and long to int is explicit because it can silently truncate.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Overloading == without overriding Equals and GetHashCode. Then a == b and a.Equals(b) can disagree, and dictionary and LINQ lookups break in ways that are very hard to debug.
  • Some operators must be declared in pairs. ==/!=, </>, <=/>=.
  • Implicit conversions that can throw. The cast is the reader's only warning, so removing it removes the warning.
  • Overloading operators to mean something unexpected. If + on your type deletes something, you have created a trap.
  • Indexers cannot be static, and they cannot be used with the null-conditional operator on the indexer name itself — though list?[0] does work.
  • && and || cannot be overloaded directly. You overload &, |, true and false instead, which is rarely worth doing.

docs.title: 1.20 — Exception Handling
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.19 Indexers and operators · Next: 1.21 IDisposable

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• throw; keeps the original stack trace. throw ex; destroys it. This is the single most-asked question in this topic.
  • finally always runs, whether an exception happened or not. That is what makes cleanup reliable.
  • Only catch what you can actually do something about. Catching everything and carrying on quietly is worse than crashing.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
An exception is how a method says "I cannot do what you asked, and I cannot carry on."

The important idea is that exceptions travel upwards. If a method throws and does not catch it, the exception passes to whoever called it, and then to whoever called them, all the way up until something catches it — or the program crashes.

That is deliberate and useful. It means the code that detects a problem does not have to be the code that decides what to do about it. A database method knows the connection failed; it has no idea whether the right response is to retry, show an error page, or give up.

docs.title: The basic shapes
docs.text:
try
{
    var result = DoRiskyThing();
}
catch (FileNotFoundException ex)      // most specific first
{
    logger.LogWarning(ex, "File missing, using defaults");
}
catch (IOException ex)                // less specific
{
    logger.LogError(ex, "IO problem");
    throw;
}
finally
{
    // ALWAYS runs — after success, after a handled exception,
    // and on the way out of an unhandled one
    connection.Close();
}

Catch blocks are checked top to bottom, and the first matching one wins. So more specific exception types must come first. If you put catch (Exception) at the top, nothing below it can ever run — and the compiler will tell you so.

docs.title: throw; versus throw ex; ⚠️
docs.text:
This is the most-asked question in the whole topic, so it is worth being able to explain precisely.

try { DoWork(); }
catch (Exception ex)
{
    LogIt(ex);
    throw ex;      // WRONG
}

throw ex; restarts the exception from this line. The stack trace — the list of method calls showing where the problem actually happened — is wiped and replaced with one starting here.

So instead of a trace pointing at the real failure five methods deep, you get one pointing at your catch block. The genuinely useful information is gone, permanently.

try { DoWork(); }
catch (Exception ex)
{
    LogIt(ex);
    throw;         // CORRECT
}

Bare throw; re-throws the same exception with its original stack trace intact.

If you only remember one thing from this note, remember this one.

There is a third option when you want to add context by wrapping:

catch (SqlException ex)
{
    throw new OrderProcessingException($"Could not save order {id}", ex);
    //                                                              ^^^^
    // Pass the original as innerException — its trace is preserved inside
}

Always pass the original exception as the inner exception when wrapping. Otherwise you have thrown away the cause.

docs.title: Exception filters — when
docs.text:
try { await CallApiAsync(); }
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
{
    return null;      // 404 is fine, we expected it
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode >= HttpStatusCode.InternalServerError)
{
    throw new UpstreamUnavailableException("The API is down", ex);
}

A filter looks like it is just a condition, and you might think you could write the same thing with an if inside the catch block. There is an important difference:

A filter is evaluated before the stack unwinds. If the filter returns false, the exception carries on as though this catch block was never there — and the stack is completely undisturbed. With catch + if + throw;, the runtime has already started unwinding, which makes debugging harder and loses some information.

Filters are also very useful for conditional logging without actually handling anything:

catch (Exception ex) when (LogAndContinue(ex))
{
    // never reached — LogAndContinue always returns false
}

static bool LogAndContinue(Exception ex) { Log(ex); return false; }

docs.title: Custom exceptions
docs.text:
public class OrderNotFoundException(Guid orderId)
    : Exception($"Order {orderId} was not found")
{
    public Guid OrderId { get; } = orderId;
}

Create one when callers might reasonably want to catch that specific case. If nobody would ever write catch (MyException), you do not need a new type — use an existing one.

Carry structured data as properties (like OrderId above) rather than only putting it in the message. That way a handler can use the value, and your logging can record it as a proper field rather than text.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
// 1. Swallowing — the worst thing in this file
try { DoWork(); }
catch { }
// The problem still happened. You just made it invisible.
// Someone will spend a day debugging this.

// 2. Catching everything at the wrong level
try { DoWork(); }
catch (Exception ex) { logger.LogError(ex, "error"); }
// Now the caller thinks it worked. Data is silently wrong.

// 3. Using exceptions for normal control flow
try { var user = GetUser(id); }
catch (NotFoundException) { user = null; }
// "Not found" is a normal outcome, not an exceptional one.
// Return null or use a Try pattern — exceptions are SLOW
// (roughly thousands of times slower than a normal return).

docs.title: Exceptions in ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
You should almost never wrap individual controller actions in try/catch. Instead you handle exceptions once, globally:

public class GlobalExceptionHandler(ILogger<GlobalExceptionHandler> logger)
    : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(
        HttpContext context, Exception ex, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        logger.LogError(ex, "Unhandled exception on {Path}", context.Request.Path);

        var problem = ex switch
        {
            OrderNotFoundException     => new ProblemDetails { Status = 404, Title = "Not found" },
            ValidationException        => new ProblemDetails { Status = 400, Title = "Invalid request" },
            UnauthorizedAccessException=> new ProblemDetails { Status = 403, Title = "Forbidden" },
            _                          => new ProblemDetails { Status = 500, Title = "Server error" }
        };

        context.Response.StatusCode = problem.Status!.Value;
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(problem, ct);
        return true;
    }
}

Notice the 500 case gives no detail. Never send exception messages or stack traces to a client — they leak table names, file paths, and library versions that help an attacker. Log the detail; return something generic. See 5.12 and 17.1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A method that handles exceptions well — notice how little it catches:

public async Task<Order> PlaceOrderAsync(CreateOrderRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Validate up front. Do NOT use exceptions to check normal input.
    if (request.Lines.Count == 0)
        throw new ArgumentException("Order must have at least one line", nameof(request));

    await using var transaction = await _db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

    try
    {
        var order = Order.Create(request);
        _db.Orders.Add(order);
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);

        await _payments.ChargeAsync(order.Total, ct);

        await transaction.CommitAsync(ct);
        return order;
    }
    catch (PaymentDeclinedException ex)
    {
        // We can genuinely handle this — roll back and convert
        // into something the caller understands.
        await transaction.RollbackAsync(ct);
        throw new OrderRejectedException(request.CustomerId, ex);
    }
    // Note: no catch(Exception). Anything else goes up to the
    // global handler, and 'await using' still rolls the transaction back.
}

Two design points worth stating in an interview:

  • The only thing caught is the one case this method can actually do something about.
  • The transaction is cleaned up by await using, not by a finally block. Disposal is more reliable and less code. See 1.21.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between throw; and throw ex;?

throw; re-throws the current exception and keeps its original stack trace, so you can still see where the problem actually happened. throw ex; throws the exception object again but resets the stack trace to start at that line, which destroys the information about the real origin. So throw ex; is almost always a bug — it turns a useful error report into a useless one. If you want to add context, throw a new exception and pass the original as the inner exception, which keeps the original trace nested inside.

Q: When does the finally block run?

Always, in every normal path — after the try block succeeds, after a catch block handles something, and while an unhandled exception is passing through on its way up. That is what makes it the right place for cleanup. The exceptions to "always" are extreme: Environment.FailFast, a stack overflow, or the process being killed. In modern C# you usually do not write finally for cleanup anyway — using and await using do it more reliably and with less code.

Q: What are exception filters and why use them over an if inside the catch?

A filter is a when clause on a catch block. The key difference from an if inside the block is timing: the filter runs before the stack unwinds. If it returns false, the exception continues on as if that catch block did not exist, and the stack is completely undisturbed — which means better debugging information. With catch-then-check-then-rethrow, unwinding has already begun. Filters are also useful for logging without handling, by calling a logging method that always returns false.

Q: Should you catch Exception?

Very rarely, and only at the top of the application — a global handler in ASP.NET Core, or the main loop of a background service — where the job is to log it and return a sensible response rather than crash the whole process. Everywhere else, catching Exception means you are claiming you can handle problems you have not thought about, including ones like out-of-memory that you certainly cannot. The rule I use is: only catch what you can genuinely do something about, and let everything else reach the one place that is designed to deal with it.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• throw ex; wipes the stack trace. Use bare throw;.
  • catch { } with an empty body hides real failures. If you genuinely intend to ignore something, log it and write a comment explaining why.
  • Exceptions are slow. Roughly thousands of times slower than a normal return. Never use them for expected outcomes like "not found" or "invalid input".
  • Catch order matters. Specific types first. catch (Exception) at the top makes everything below unreachable.
  • Never send exception details to a client. Messages and stack traces leak internal structure that is useful to an attacker.
  • OperationCanceledException is normal, not an error. When a request is cancelled you will see it, and logging it as an error creates noise. See 2.14.
  • Exceptions inside a finally block replace the original one. The real error disappears. Keep finally blocks simple and non-throwing.
  • An unobserved exception in an async void method crashes the process. See 2.15.

docs.title: 1.21 — IDisposable, using, and Finalizers
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.20 Exceptions · Next: 1.22 Anonymous types, dynamic, var

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• The garbage collector handles memory. It does not handle file handles, sockets, or database connections. IDisposable exists for those.
  • using guarantees Dispose() gets called, even if an exception is thrown. It compiles down to a try/finally.
  • Finalizers are a last-resort safety net, not a cleanup mechanism. They make objects live longer and they run at an unpredictable time. Avoid writing them.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
.NET's garbage collector automatically frees memory you are no longer using. That covers most things.

But some resources are not memory. A file handle, a network socket, a database connection — these are given out by the operating system, and the operating system has a limited number of them. The garbage collector does not know or care about them.

Worse, the GC runs whenever it feels like it. It might be seconds or minutes before it gets round to your object. In the meantime, that file stays locked and that database connection stays taken out of the pool.

IDisposable is the answer: a standard way for a type to say "I am holding something that needs releasing — tell me when you are done."

The rule to remember: if a type implements IDisposable, you are responsible for disposing it.

docs.title: The using statement
docs.text:
using (var stream = new FileStream("data.txt", FileMode.Open))
{
    // work with the stream
}
// Dispose() is called here — guaranteed

The compiler expands this into:

var stream = new FileStream("data.txt", FileMode.Open);
try
{
    // work with the stream
}
finally
{
    stream?.Dispose();      // runs even if an exception was thrown
}

That finally is the whole point. Even if the code inside throws, even if you return early, Dispose() still runs.

docs.title: using declarations (C# 8)
docs.text:
Since C# 8 you can drop the braces. The object is disposed at the end of the enclosing scope:

public async Task<string> ReadAsync(string path)
{
    using var stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);
    using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);

    return await reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    // Both disposed here, in reverse order: reader first, then stream
}

This removes a lot of nesting. Note the reverse order — the last one created is disposed first, which is what you want since reader depends on stream.

docs.title: IAsyncDisposable and await using
docs.text:
Some cleanup needs to be asynchronous — flushing a buffer to disk, sending a final network message. Calling a synchronous Dispose that blocks on async work is a good way to deadlock or starve the thread pool.

await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
// DisposeAsync() is awaited at the end of scope

If a type offers both, prefer await using. In ASP.NET Core, blocking a thread is expensive — see 19.12.

docs.title: Implementing it — the simple case
docs.text:
Most of the time, your class just holds other disposable things. Then it is easy:

public sealed class ReportGenerator : IDisposable
{
    private readonly FileStream _output;

    public ReportGenerator(string path) => _output = File.Create(path);

    public void Dispose() => _output.Dispose();
}

Note sealed. If nobody can inherit from your class, you do not need the complicated pattern below. Sealing is the easiest way to keep disposal simple, and it is what Microsoft recommends.

docs.title: The full dispose pattern — only when inheritance is possible
docs.text:
If your class is not sealed and holds unmanaged resources directly, you need the full pattern:

public class NativeBuffer : IDisposable
{
    private IntPtr _handle;          // unmanaged — the GC knows nothing about this
    private FileStream? _stream;     // managed — the GC handles its memory
    private bool _disposed;

    public void Dispose()
    {
        Dispose(disposing: true);
        GC.SuppressFinalize(this);   // we cleaned up, so skip the finalizer
    }

    protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)
    {
        if (_disposed) return;

        if (disposing)
        {
            // Called from Dispose(). Safe to touch other managed objects.
            _stream?.Dispose();
        }

        // Always clean up unmanaged resources
        if (_handle != IntPtr.Zero)
        {
            Marshal.FreeHGlobal(_handle);
            _handle = IntPtr.Zero;
        }

        _disposed = true;
    }

    ~NativeBuffer() => Dispose(disposing: false);   // finalizer — safety net only
}

Why does disposing exist? Because a finalizer runs on a separate thread at an unpredictable time, and by then the other managed objects your class references may already have been collected. Touching them would be a bug. So when disposing is false (meaning we came from the finalizer), you only clean up unmanaged things.

Why GC.SuppressFinalize? Because if Dispose() already did the work, running the finalizer later is pointless — and finalizers are expensive. See below.

In practice, you will almost never write this. Wrap unmanaged handles in SafeHandle, which handles all of it correctly for you.

docs.title: Why finalizers are bad
docs.text:
An object with a finalizer costs significantly more:

  1. When it is created, it goes on a special "needs finalizing" queue.
  2. When the GC would normally collect it, it cannot — it has to run the finalizer first.
  3. So the object is promoted to the next generation and survives longer.
  4. A separate finalizer thread runs the method at some unpredictable later point.
  5. Only on the next garbage collection is the memory actually freed.

So a finalizer means your object survives at least two collections instead of one. Add a finalizer to a frequently created type and you can measurably hurt performance.

A finalizer is a safety net for when someone forgets to call Dispose. It is not a cleanup strategy.

docs.title: Who disposes what in ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
This comes up a lot. The DI container disposes services it created, when their scope ends:

builder.Services.AddScoped<MyDisposableService>();
// Container creates it, container disposes it at the end of the request.
// You do NOT dispose it yourself.

builder.Services.AddSingleton(new MyDisposableService());
// YOU created this instance and handed it over.
// The container does NOT dispose it. It is yours to manage.

And the important exception: never dispose an HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory. The factory manages the underlying handler's lifetime, and disposing it defeats the entire mechanism. See 19.10.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is IDisposable for, when we already have a garbage collector?

The garbage collector manages memory, and it does that well. But it knows nothing about resources that are not memory — file handles, sockets, database connections, operating system handles. Those are limited, and holding them too long causes real problems like locked files and exhausted connection pools. The GC also runs at an unpredictable time, so even for things it could eventually clean up, "eventually" is not good enough. IDisposable gives you a standard way to say "release this now", and using guarantees it happens even if an exception is thrown.

Q: What does the using statement compile to?

A try/finally. The object is created before the try, and Dispose() is called in the finally block with a null check. That is why it works even when the body throws or returns early. The C# 8 using declaration form without braces does the same thing, disposing at the end of the enclosing scope, in reverse order of creation.

Q: What is a finalizer and when would you write one?

A finalizer is a method the garbage collector calls before reclaiming an object, written as ~ClassName(). Almost never write one. It makes the object survive at least one extra garbage collection, because the GC has to put it on a queue and run the finalizer on a separate thread before it can free the memory. It also runs at an unpredictable time, and by then other managed objects it references may already be gone. The only legitimate use is as a last-resort safety net for an unmanaged handle held directly — and even then, SafeHandle does the job properly and you should use that instead.

Q: What is GC.SuppressFinalize and why is it in the dispose pattern?

It tells the garbage collector not to bother running this object's finalizer. You call it at the end of Dispose() because if Dispose has already cleaned everything up, running the finalizer afterwards is pure waste — and finalizers are expensive, keeping the object alive for an extra collection cycle. So it turns the "someone forgot to dispose" penalty back off when they did remember.

Q: In ASP.NET Core, who is responsible for disposing services?

The container disposes anything it created, when the owning scope ends — so a scoped service is disposed at the end of the request and a singleton at application shutdown. But if you register an instance you built yourself, with AddSingleton(new Thing()), the container does not take ownership and you have to manage it. The other case worth knowing is HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory — you should never dispose those, because the factory is managing the underlying handler pool.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting to dispose. No error, no warning at runtime — just leaked handles and exhausted connection pools under load.
  • Disposing something the container owns. Causes "cannot access a disposed object" on the next request.
  • Disposing an HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory. Defeats the whole point of the factory.
  • Writing a finalizer when you do not need one. It makes every instance more expensive and delays collection.
  • Calling Dispose() inside a finalizer without the disposing flag. The managed objects you are touching may already be collected.
  • Dispose() must be safe to call more than once. The guard flag exists for this reason; throwing on a second call breaks callers.
  • A synchronous Dispose that blocks on async work can deadlock or starve the thread pool. Implement IAsyncDisposable instead.
  • using on a null variable is fine. The generated code null-checks it.

docs.title: 1.22 — Anonymous Types, dynamic, and var
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 1. C# Language Fundamentals Prev: 1.21 IDisposable · Next: 1.23 Attributes and reflection

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• var is still fully type-safe. The compiler works out the type and fixes it. var x = 5; and int x = 5; produce identical code.
  • dynamic genuinely turns off type checking until runtime. Everything becomes a runtime error waiting to happen.
  • Anonymous types (new { Name = "Ada" }) are real, compiler-generated classes. Useful inside a method, useless outside one.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These three get grouped together because they all look like "the type is not specified". Only one of them actually is.

  • var — "compiler, work out the type for me". Type safety is completely intact.
  • dynamic — "do not check anything, sort it out at runtime". Type safety is gone.
  • anonymous type — "make me a throwaway class here and now".

The interview question is almost always var versus dynamic. The answer is that they are not remotely similar, and confusing them is a red flag.

docs.title: var — type inference
docs.text:
The compiler looks at the right-hand side and works out the type. Once it has, that type is fixed forever.

var number = 5;              // compiler decides: int
var name = "Ada";            // compiler decides: string
var list = new List<Order>();// compiler decides: List<Order>

number = "hello";            // COMPILE ERROR — number is an int, permanently

var x = 5; and int x = 5; compile to exactly the same IL. There is no runtime cost and no loss of safety. var is purely about how much you type.

Rules:

  • Only for local variables. Not for fields, parameters, or return types.
  • You must initialise it in the same statement — the compiler needs something to infer from.
  • Cannot be null on its own: var x = null; fails, because null does not identify a type.

When to use it is a style question, and teams differ. A reasonable position:

var order = new Order();                       // obvious — the type is right there
var orders = new List<Dictionary<string, int>>();  // obvious, and saves a lot of typing

var result = ProcessThings();                  // NOT obvious — what does this return?
IReadOnlyList<Order> result = ProcessThings(); // clearer

The test: can a reader tell the type from this one line? If yes, var is fine. If they would have to go and look at the method signature, write the type out.

docs.title: dynamic — no compile-time checking at all
docs.text:
dynamic value = GetSomething();
value.AnyMethodAtAll();          // compiles fine, whatever it is
value.ThisDoesNotExist();        // ALSO compiles fine
                                 // → RuntimeBinderException when it runs

The compiler stops checking entirely. Member lookup happens while the program is running, using the Dynamic Language Runtime.

The costs are real:

  • No compile-time errors. Every typo becomes a runtime crash.
  • No IntelliSense. Your editor cannot help you.
  • Slower. Every call goes through a lookup and caching mechanism.
  • No refactoring safety. Rename a property and dynamic call sites are silently missed.

When is it justified? Genuinely rarely:

  • Talking to COM objects, like Office automation
  • Interoperating with a dynamic language such as IronPython
  • Truly unknown JSON shapes — though JsonNode or JsonElement is usually better

If you find yourself reaching for dynamic in normal application code, there is almost always a better answer: an interface, a generic, or pattern matching.

docs.title: dynamic vs object vs var
docs.text:
This comparison is a common question:

object o = "hello";
o.Length;              // COMPILE ERROR — object has no Length. Cast first.

dynamic d = "hello";
d.Length;              // Compiles. Works at runtime. Returns 5.
d.Nonsense();          // Compiles. Throws at runtime.

var v = "hello";
v.Length;              // Compiles. v IS a string — full IntelliSense.
v.Nonsense();          // COMPILE ERROR — caught immediately.
Checked at compile time? Needs a cast? IntelliSense? var Yes No Yes object Yes Yes No, until cast dynamic No No No

docs.title: Anonymous types
docs.text:
var person = new { Name = "Ada", Age = 36 };
Console.WriteLine(person.Name);      // fully typed, IntelliSense works

The compiler generates a real class behind the scenes with read-only properties, a value-based Equals and GetHashCode, and a helpful ToString.

Their limitation is that the type has no name you can write. So you cannot return one from a method, put one in a field, or use it as a parameter type. It only works inside the method that created it — which is exactly why var is required for them.

Their main real use is LINQ projections:

var summary = orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, o.CustomerName, o.Total })   // only these 3 columns
    .ToList();

In Entity Framework this is genuinely useful, because it means the generated SQL only selects the three columns you actually need instead of the whole row. See 13.15.

But once the data leaves the method, use a record instead:

public record OrderSummary(Guid Id, string CustomerName, decimal Total);

public IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary> GetSummaries() =>
    _db.Orders
       .Where(o => o.Total > 100)
       .Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.Customer.Name, o.Total))
       .ToList();

Same SQL benefit, but now it has a name, it can be returned, and it appears properly in Swagger.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between var and dynamic?

They are completely different despite looking similar. var is compile-time type inference — the compiler works out the type from the initialiser and fixes it permanently, so you get full type checking, IntelliSense and no runtime cost at all. var x = 5; compiles to exactly the same thing as int x = 5;. dynamic switches type checking off entirely: member lookup is deferred to runtime, so any typo compiles fine and throws when it executes, there is no IntelliSense, and every call has overhead. var is about convenience; dynamic is about giving up safety, and it is rarely the right choice.

Q: When is dynamic actually appropriate?

When the type genuinely is not known until runtime and there is no reasonable alternative — COM interop like automating Excel, interoperating with a dynamic language, or handling completely unstructured data. Even for JSON, JsonNode or JsonElement is usually a better answer because it gives you a real API. In ordinary application code, reaching for dynamic is normally a sign that an interface or a generic would solve the problem properly.

Q: What is an anonymous type and where would you use one?

It is a compiler-generated class created inline with new { Name = "Ada" }. The compiler produces a real type with read-only properties and value-based equality, but that type has no name you can write, so it cannot leave the method it was created in. That makes them useful for LINQ projections — selecting only the three columns you need from a query so that Entity Framework generates narrower SQL. As soon as the data needs to cross a method boundary, a record is the better choice, because it has a name, it can be returned, and it shows up properly in API documentation.

Q: Does var have any runtime cost?

None at all. It is purely a compile-time convenience. The compiler determines the concrete type and emits exactly the same IL as if you had typed the type out yourself. The variable is just as strongly typed either way.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Thinking var is weakly typed. It is not. The type is fixed at compile time.
  • dynamic turns every typo into a runtime crash. No compiler help, no IntelliSense, no safe refactoring.
  • Overusing var hurts readability. var result = Process(); tells a reader nothing.
  • Anonymous types cannot escape the method. No returning them, no fields, no parameters.
  • Anonymous type equality is by value, but only for the exact same shape. Two anonymous types with the same properties in a different order are different types.
  • dynamic silently defeats extension methods. Extension methods are resolved at compile time, so calling one on a dynamic fails at runtime.
  • var x = null; does not compile. You need string? x = null; or a cast.
